summary.source_abstract: Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been used to generate mutants in both research work and in industrial practice. However, there has been no comprehensive empirical study of their performance for this increasingly important LLM-based Software Engineering application. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study evaluating BugFarm and LLMorpheus (the two state-of-the-art LLM-based approaches), alongside seven LLMs using our newly designed prompt, including both leading open- and closed-source models, on 851 real bugs from two Java real-world bug benchmarks. Our results reveal that, compared to existing rule-based approaches, LLMs generate more diverse mutants, that are behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, with 111.29% higher fault detection. That is, 87.98% (for LLMs) vs. 41.64% (for rule-based); an increase of 46.34 percentage points. Nevertheless, our results also reveal that these impressive results for improved effectiveness come at a cost: the LLM-generated mutants have worse non-compilability, duplication, and equivalent mutant rates by 26.60, 10.14, and 3.51 percentage points, respectively. These findings are immediately actionable for both research and practice. They allow practitioners to have greater confidence in deploying LLM-based mutation, while researchers now have a baseline for the state-of-the-art, with which they can research techniques to further improve effectiveness and reduce cost.

# LLM-era mutants raise fault detection and raise equivalence at the same time, and equivalence is declared undecidable

Admitted in round 58 from the shokuknow `corpus-expansion-1` package
(`merge/tameshi/knowledge/corpus/knowledge/llm-mutant-equivalence-cost.md`, staged ids S156/S165,
re-pointed by document to S286/S287 after the id-collision check; package text adapted before
landing — this entry is the lane's own re-grounding, not a byte copy).

## What the sources state

- S286 evaluates LLM-generated mutants against rule-based ones on 851 real
  bugs from two Java bug benchmarks: the LLM mutants are "more diverse ...
  behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, with 111.29% higher
  fault detection", but "the LLM-generated mutants have worse non-compilability,
  duplication, and equivalent mutant rates by 26.60, 10.14, and 3.51 percentage
  points, respectively" (§Abstract, verified present in the copy opened 2026-10-30).
- S287 states the equivalence class — "等价变异体：变异后的程序与原始程序在功能上完全相同" — and records
  the hazards of that class: it "影响变异分数计算的精确度" (degrades the precision of the
  mutation score), and deciding equivalence is undecidable in general:
  "判断等价变异体是不可判定问题：不存在一个自动算法完美解决" (extract lines 230-241; the class
  definition itself is line 231).

## What this means for the lane's survivor classes

- **A survivor is not yet a test hole.** The lane's survivor classes (its
  own arm-class matrix, and the B5 / D2 / D10 survivors) are all cases where
  a mutant was *not killed*. S286 shows that in an LLM-mutant setting a
  materially larger share of un-killed mutants are equivalent. Inference: an
  LLM-era survivor must be classified against an equivalence witness before
  it is counted as a gap in the suite — the same non-equivalence witness the
  lane already requires for rule-based mutants.
- **Three counters, not one.** S286 reports non-compilability, duplication
  and equivalence as three separate rates. The lane's F1 note (compile and
  runtime errors excluded from the score, per its held S001) means a
  non-compilating LLM mutant must not silently enter the denominator.
  Inference: an LLM-era sweep needs three counters.
- **The two literatures agree on the hazard.** S286 quantifies the
  equivalence rate in English; S287 states the same hazard in Chinese and
  adds an explicit statement that the problem admits no automatic solution.

## Boundary of this entry

- S286 is measured on Java and on real-world bug benchmarks; the lane's legs
  are one JavaScript gate and one bash gate. The transfer is **not
  measured**: no lane sweep has produced an LLM-generated mutant yet, and
  the entry supplies the counting contract, not a measurement.
- Equivalence stays undecidable (S287): a witness is per-mutant evidence
  (an input where the mutant and the original differ), never a general
  decision procedure. The lane's 1-minimality witness
  (`corpus/knowledge/delta-debugging-minimization-contract.md`) reduces a
  failing case; it does not decide equivalence.
- The F9 pilot move (a bounded LLM-mutant pilot with an independent outcome
  check) remains unmeasured; this entry does not close it.

# Arm-class matrix — JS (r2) × bash (r3) (TAMESHI-R4-1)

Run date 2026-10-14. Lane: tameshi (round 4; plan `tameshi-shokunin/plans/round-4.plan.md`,
axis: calibration — suite-vs-arm completeness across the two worked cases). Sources: the two
mutation-case notes in this corpus — `knowledge/mutation-case-kimi-census.md` (r2, kumitate
`kimi-census.mjs`, mutants D1–D10) and `knowledge/mutation-case-kagi-census.md` (r3, kagi
`surface-census.sh`, mutants B1–B10). Substrates kumitate-shokunin + kagi-shokunin
**read-only**: three anchor re-reads plus two hermetic `--selftest` pulses on the pinned
bytes (§12); both trees porcelain-empty after; this note is the only file written by the run
(the corpus/README row and the `LOG.md` entry fold in at lane review).

Anchors: **O** = observation (file:line, command output, or a re-quoted measured table cell);
**I** = inference; **U** = unknown. `kimi-census.mjs:NNN` =
`kumitate-shokunin/scripts/kimi-census.mjs` @ sha256 `83016d45…4f426`, kumitate `175de6ba`;
`surface-census.sh:NNN` = `kagi-shokunin/corpus/surface-census.sh` @ sha256 `275d8294…53009f`,
kagi `fecee87`. Both pins re-verified held 2026-10-14 (§12).

Method (O): this note runs no new mutants. It re-cuts the two notes' measured tables by **arm
class** — a surface the suite either reads through an assert or does not — and states per
class where the cases agree and where they disagree (the plan's anti-claim: a disagreement is
the finding, never averaged). Ledger verdicts and failing-case counts are O (re-quoted from
the note tables; the round-3b audit independently re-swept both cases end-to-end through
`tools/mutate-and-run.sh`, per-defect verdicts identical to both tables — `LOG.md` round-3b
`TAMESHI-B3`). **Class membership is I** — a reading of measured cells, not a new
measurement. Classes are surfaces, not a partition: D2 and B10 are (deliberately) listed
under two rows each.

## 0. Headline

## 2. Row A — Verdict paths (exit + verdict line as read by callers)

**JS.** O: the DRIFT verdict is asserted by prefix plus kind plus a `members=` substring
(`kimi-census.mjs:498-499`); the **only** whole-verdict-line equality anywhere is the CLEAN
line (`lastLine(r) === 'KIMI_CENSUS: CLEAN (members=49 checked=49 chain=3 info=4)'`,
`:511-512`), with `startsWith('KIMI_CENSUS: CLEAN')` at `:642` and `includes(…)` tiers
elsewhere (`:535-536`). Positive controls: D3 and D1 each die on 16 cases *because* the exact
baseline line breaks under them — the equality assert is load-bearing. Measured gap: **D2
survives** (43/43) with the tail past the prefix changed — one fewer listed id and `+23 more`
instead of `+22 more` on a ≥6-finding input; the max findings any suite run reaches is 2
against the cap of 6, and because the DRIFT assert is prefix-based, even a 6-finding case
would not pin the tail.

**bash.** O: every case asserts `exit + one substring token` (`run_case`, `surface-census.sh:747-760`;
the token may be empty). There is **no** whole-line or prefix assert anywhere in the selftest

the CLEAN line's `ok=` field moved (`:862`); off-suite: `ok=0` vs pristine `ok=1`, both
exit 0.

(exit + the pinned token/prefix) is protected — all 16 kills are read through it — and both
lose a mutant confined to the verdict line's *unasserted remainder*. **Disagreement (stated,
not averaged):** the pin styles differ — JS pins one entire verdict line by equality and
tiers down through prefix/substring for others; bash pins no line weight above a substring,
anywhere. The two gap shapes are therefore different in kind: JS's is truncation arithmetic
inside a verdict line (`+N more`), bash's is a field of a summary line read by no case.

## 3. Row B — Fail-closed arms

**JS.** O: D8 (`failClosed` `return 2` → `return 1`, `:396`) is killed by exactly the three
fail-closed cases, and those cases assert more than the exit: `--root /nonexistent` and the
unreadable root assert exit 2 **and** the `KIMI_CENSUS: FAIL-CLOSED (KIMI_ROOT_MISSING`
prefix (`:777-779`, `:789-790`), the `--json` case asserts `j.verdict === 'FAIL-CLOSED'` +
`j.fatal.kind` + empty totals (`:800-802`); the suite also declares its arm enum
(`FAIL_CLOSED_KINDS = ['KIMI_ROOT_MISSING']`, `:148`) and meta-checks that every declared arm
fired (`:840-842`). The measured species here is **environment failure** (root missing,
unreadable, json variant).

**bash.** O: B8 (`die` exit 2 → 1, `:85`) is killed by cases 13 `malformed-row` (wants
exit=2 + token `bad kind`) and 14 `fused-shape-row` (rc==2 + `too many fields`). The exit-2
species here is **malformed committed data** — the census's own taxonomy calls it "not a
verdict". The "cannot measure" species sits elsewhere by design: `sqlite-unavailable` exits
**1** with the verdict-shaped `SHAPE UNVERIFIED` line, and case 10 pins it with substrings
plus the exact count `unverified=3` (`:782`) — the count that also killed B7.

**Agreement (narrow, measured):** a 2→1 exit-map edit dies in both cases. **Disagreement
(stated, not averaged):** the two cases' exit-2 case sets guard different arm species
(environment failure in JS; malformed-input refusal in bash), and bash's environment-class
condition is deliberately *not* an exit-2 arm at all — it is an exit-1 verdict pinned by
substrings/count. So "fail-closed arms are protected" is true of the pair only for the shared
exit-map property; the arm inventories behind it are not the same inventory.

## 4. Row C — Counts (declared↔live, floors, tallies, exact-count strings)

**JS.** O: D1 (counted `18`→`17`, `:105`) killed on 16 cases — the edit desyncs a duplicate
table (`ENUMERABLE.childCount` `:137`) and breaks the green fixture itself; the tripwires
include the exact baseline counts and the literal `'19 children, 18 declared'`. D6 (declared
floor `0o600`→`0o644`, `:124`) killed on the two loose-mode cases, with the FIFO case as

(`0o500` vs `0o700`; `0o400` vs `0o600`), which discriminate "contains the floor" from

**bash.** O: B2 (rows floor `-ge`→`-gt`, `:435`) killed on both exit-0 green fixtures (the
fixture's part table sits exactly at the floor); B7 (`N_UNVERIFIED + 1` → `+ 2`, `:405-406`)
killed on case 10 by the exact substring `unverified=3` — the suite's only exact-count string
with a case behind it. Surviving count-shaped surface: B10 (row D).

**Agreement:** a count edit that an assert reads dies in both cases, floors included.
**Disagreement (stated, not averaged):** (O) width — a count edit in JS kills up to 16/43
(shared in-memory fixtures + exact-line asserts), in bash at most 2/16 (fresh fixture per
case + exit/token asserts; the note's §4 mechanism (I)). (O) assert exactness — JS reads

substring plus floor-token cases (`rows part 0`). (O) both cases nevertheless lose one
count-shaped mutant to the same place: a count the suite never reads (D10/B10 → row D).

## 5. Row D — Reported-but-unasserted surfaces

**JS survivors.** O: D2 — the verdict line's tail past the asserted prefix (row A). D10 —

## 6. Row E — Unreached arms

(root-stray reporting loop deleted) died on exactly the three root-enumeration cases with no
other case moving (arm isolation), D5 (chain presence gate) died on a singleton. Nothing in

**bash: one instance.** O: B4 (symlink arm deleted) killed on case 07 — but the exit code
still matched and the token assert carried the kill (a reached arm pinned by one token). B5
(exec x-bit arm deleted, `:214-217`) **survived** 16/16: no case ever exercises a row
declared `exec` whose file lost its x bit — the fixture creates that row at `chmod 755` and
no case strips it (the only chmod sites are `:521-588`, `:704-717`, `:768`; `-x ` occurs once

`SURFACE OK … (exec 644)` exit 0 where pristine reports `SURFACE DIVERGED … no execute bit`
exit 1. Nothing reaches the arm, so no implementation of it — right or wrong — can move the
suite.

**Disagreement (the anti-claim's finding, stated not averaged):** same defect class — a
deleted arm — yields 2/2 kills in JS and 1/2 in bash; across the four dropped-arm mutants of
the 20, 3/4 died, and the survivor is the one arm with no case behind it. The unit that
disagrees is the **arm**, not the language: JS's suite reached both arms it was handed;
bash's suite reached one of two. Reachability is per-arm and must be measured per-arm
(B5's shape matches kagi's own F-2 refusal-path-without-a-case hole, cited in `SKILL.md:451-456`).
**Confidence:** one measured instance (B5) in one lane → proposed, not general; JS's D4/D5
are counter-instances that bound the class rather than contradict it.

Boundary remark (case-side, different species): bash cases 15/16 `skip-case …
substrate-absent` performed no execution yet sit inside `PASS (16 cases)` (O §12) — a
*declared, counted* abstention, not an unreached arm; the hermetic case set on this host is
14+2. The JS recorded runs abstained from nothing. Do not conflate skipped cases with
unreached arms: the skip is loud in the case grammar, the unreached arm is silent.

## 7. Row F — Coordinated edits

**No mutants in either case.** JS U1: a coordinated edit of both count tables (`:105` **and**
`:137`) was not probed; the note's (I) — the literal-count asserts would still kill it. bash

experiments, and the pair's only agreement is that the method stops here (JS U2 / bash scope:
single-text edits, no reordering, no timing mutants). Not admitted; not averaged.

## 8. Row G — Behavior predicates (added row)

Not one of the assignment's six classes; added so that all 20 mutants have a row (without it
D3, D9, B1, B3, B6, B9 are unplaced). These are single-edit logic/invariant mutants that are

# Partial artifacts do not rehabilitate failed seats

This is a same-ground calibration repair, not a newly explored province.
Round21 retained two Markdown reports from provider-dead seats:
`ProfileBashTsukuroiCensus` and `V01WitnessTests`. Its appended erratum
preserves the original wrong inference and the actual terminal statuses.
The reusable rule is to separate three observations:

| Observation | What it establishes | What it cannot establish |
|---|---|---|
| registered exact name/agent ID/role | which dispatched identity belongs in the denominator | whether execution completed |
| retained terminal callback status | declared completed or failed outcome for that identity | cryptographic provider authenticity |
| Markdown report exists | an artifact was written, possibly partial | successful completion |

`tools/wave-accounting.py` checks a digest-pinned bundle, nonempty exact
membership, unique agent identities, final status vocabulary, identity/role
agreement, no declared replacement, and caller totals. It inventories
failed-with-report seats without changing their status. Report prose and
file presence never supply the completed count. It reads no live provider
or orchestration configuration and cannot authenticate an edited callback
snapshot whose expected digest is also intentionally replaced.

The frozen round22 bundle is an explicit projection, not the original raw
callback stream: `derivation.json` pins the source revision and source-file
hashes. Completed callbacks that omitted `replaced` receive `false` from
the explicit round21 no-replacement declaration, not from treating an absent
field as independent proof. Reports are a frozen basename-existence census;
their contents are not required to establish the callback count.

Reproduce from the lane root:

```sh
python3 tools/wave-accounting.py --selftest
python3 .ufo/evidence/round-22/measure.py --repo "$PWD"
python3 tools/wave-accounting.py --bundle .ufo/evidence/round-22/bundle.json --expected .ufo/evidence/round-22/expected.json --json
python3 tools/wave-accounting.py --bundle .ufo/evidence/round-22/wrong-count-bundle.json --expected .ufo/evidence/round-22/wrong-count-expected.json --json
```

The last command is deliberately red: only the preserved wrong claimed
wave2 totals differ from the corrected bundle; the expected digest matches
that wrong-count input, so the intended failure is `TOTAL_MISMATCH`, not
snapshot corruption. The final verification receipt records observed exits,
streams, instrument hashes and measured commit rather than borrowing a
historical success.

Keep denominators separate: eight synthetic rejection predicates are
capability discrimination, the complete retained population is146 seats,
and the original mistake class has two false-positive instances. Eight
tests do not mean eight historical defects; selftest green is not outside
claim admission, independent promotion evidence, or provider authentication.

# Re-computing the mutant suite is a consistency bug; a pinned long-standing suite is the comparison device

## What the sources state

- S276: "Much previous work implicitly assumed it to be sufficient to
  re-compute mutant suites per release. Sadly, this makes mutation results
  inconsistent; mutant scores from each release cannot be directly
  compared"; the relevance of a mutant suite "will naturally degrade over
  time" — measured at "143,500 mutants in 4 non-trivial systems finding
  that, on overage, 52% degrade" — with a mutant-brittleness measure and a
  path to consistent-by-construction long-standing suites.
- S275: "around 30% of mutants are commit-relevant"; "by selecting only
  subsuming commit relevant mutants, we reduce the number of mutants
  requiring analysis by around 93% on average", with "69% of the mutants"
  located "outside the changed methods".

## What this means for the lane's re-sweep cadence

- **The lane's current cadence is the thing S276 criticises.** The lane's F7
  next move is "pin-level cadence only → per-leg reuse decisions
  classified". S276's point is that the choice is not between "recompute
  everything" and "recompute nothing" — it is between a *stable* suite
  whose relevance decays and a *fresh* suite whose numbers cannot be
  compared with the last run. Inference: the lane's pin-level cadence (S101)
  is the "stable suite" branch; its cost is that relevance decays silently,
  and its benefit is that scores stay comparable. The lane should record
  which branch it is on, because the two branches fail differently.
- **Commit relevance is a per-leg reuse decision with a measured size.**
  S275's ≈93% reduction is measured on Java class modules; the lane's legs
  are JavaScript and bash gates. Inference: the *shape* of the decision
  transfers (which changed lines, and which mutants depend on them); the
  *magnitude* does not, and is **not measured** for the lane.
- **What is still open.** The lane's F7 measurement — "per-leg reuse
  decisions classified" — is not made here. These two sources define the
  two candidate policies precisely enough to classify against; they do not
  perform the classification.

## Boundary of this entry

- Both sources are Java studies. The lane's own legs are JS and bash; the
  numbers are not transferred.
- S275's ACM copy is access-controlled (HTTP 403 on this round's re-open);
  the opened artefact is the author's camera-ready, and the row cites the
  canonical DOI.
- Adoption note (round 53): staged as `merge/tameshi` entry with rows
  S161/S162; adopted with the registry's own ids S275/S276 (append-only
  continuation; staged ids S161–S255 stay reserved by document). Both
  sources were re-opened by the lane L1 on 2026-10-27; the staged quotes
  re-located verbatim in the round's copies before the rows were written.

# A reduced fixture states its minimality witness and its cost in test runs

Admitted in round 50 from the shokuknow `corpus-expansion-1` package (staged S167, theme F6), re-grounded on
the lane's own fetch; the package's text was edited before landing (14 edits, `.ufo/waves/round-50/w1/T50ScribePkgDD.md`
`## Required edits`), and one of its two claims was refused (below).

## What the source states

- **The minimality criterion.** §I: the algorithm "is fed with a failing test case, which it simplifies by
  successive testing. It stops when a minimal test case is reached, where removing any single input entity
  would cause the failure to disappear." Definition 10 (§III-A) states n-minimality formally, and
  Proposition 11 (§III-C) states that ddmin's result "is 1-minimal in the sense of definition 10".
- **The cost is reported in test runs, per reduction.** §I: "After 57 tests, the original 896-line HTML input
  is reduced to the minimal failing test case"; §IV-B (Fig. 11): "After 82 test runs (or 21 minutes), only 3 out
  of 95 user actions are left". The Abstract reports the case study's total: "The case study required 139
  automated test runs, or 35 minutes on a 500 MHz PC". Inference: 82 + 57 = 139, so the total is most plausibly the
  two reductions summed; the paper does not say so. The paper is not consistent about the HTML run: §I ties the 57 tests
  to the minimal `<SELECT>` case, while §V-A reports "26 steps" for the reduction to the `<SELECT>` tag; the lane reads the
  57 as the 896-line run of Fig. 12 and states that reading as its own (`.ufo/waves/round-50/w2/T50W2ScoutS271.md`).

## What it means for the lane

- **The witness is a removal that loses the failure.** A reduced fixture is 1-minimal when removing any single
  unit makes the kill disappear. The direction matters: the witness is not an entity whose removal restores a
  failure. The lane's round-50 counter checks exactly this, unit by unit, on the emitted case
  (`.ufo/evidence/round-50/c2/measure.py`, docstring "minimal").
- **A reduction without its run count is not comparable.** Inference: the lane should report runs spent next to
  units removed, per reduction, and compare like with like — the source's 57 is one reduction (896 lines to 1),
  139 is, on the inference above, two reductions summed. The lane's own earlier datum, round 29's "171 oracle tests" for a reduction that
  kept nothing (`corpus/knowledge/survivor-fixture-minimization.md:53`), is a spent cost with no reduction, so it
  is not a counterpart to 57.
- **What is new against the lane's holdings.** The lane already held the 1-minimal criterion as a tier-B
  restatement (S024, `corpus/knowledge/survivor-fixture-minimization.md:3,16`). This entry adds the tier-A origin,
  the formal definition and guarantee (Definition 10, Proposition 11), and a published per-reduction cost datum.
- **B5 stays where round 29 left it.** The lane's B5 probe was tried: ddmin "made 171 oracle tests and kept
  nothing" because B5 is masked under the pinned declaration (`corpus/knowledge/survivor-fixture-minimization.md:53,57`).

  (`corpus/knowledge/fixture-shrinking-pilot.md`); the F6 status line is `corpus/README.md` `## Round 50`, not this entry.

## Refused from the package

- The package attributed "139 automated test runs, or 35 minutes" to the 896-line reduction. The source gives 57

- The source's inputs are a web browser's HTML input, recorded user actions, GCC and fuzz inputs — not a test

# Executable self-assessment rows: claims with checks

A standing capability row says what a tool can do and quotes what its command printed. A standing
axis row states a score. Each is a claim about the repository at some revision, not a timeless fact.
Give the claim a check: run the row's own command at the same revision and compare the values the
row states with the values the command prints.

When the tool changes and the row does not, the row goes stale. Stale means "needs a fresh check";
it does not by itself prove the row wrong, and a dated row that names its measured revision may
still be true of that revision. A re-check either confirms the values or shows they need a new
statement.

## What the sources say, and what this entry infers

The sources describe executable examples in three language ecosystems:

- **S055, Python `doctest`, module introduction:** "To check that a module's docstrings are
  up-to-date by verifying that all interactive examples still work as documented." Location: first
  common-use bullet, <https://docs.python.org/3/library/doctest.html>.
- **S095, Go Blog, §Output comments:** "The test passes if the test's output matches its output
  comment." Location: <https://go.dev/blog/examples>; §Introduction also says examples are
  "verified by running them as tests."
- **S096, rustdoc book, §Documentation tests:** "rustdoc supports executing your documentation
  examples as tests. This makes sure that examples within your documentation are up to date and
  working." Location: <https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/write-documentation/documentation-tests.html>.

Those are the sources' claims about documentation examples. **Inference in this entry:** a
SCORECARD row that quotes a command's output is a documentation example of the lane's own tools,
so the same remedy applies: execute the quoted command and compare. The language sources do not
establish the SCORECARD rule; the local rule comes from round 31's frozen contract and counter.

Adjacent prior art (read-only, sibling lane): kumitate-shokunin re-derives its own SCORECARD terms
with `scripts/proxy-check.mjs` (`corpus/knowledge/executable-scorecard.md` at kumitate
`9b33e03e`; seat ConnectorOverlap). It recomputes kumitate's own frozen terms from its own tree;
tameshi's check runs each row's quoted command instead. Cite, do not copy.

## Round 31's concrete check

C1 is a calibration claim over the standing `SCORECARD.md` rows. The frozen set is the ten rows of
the `| Capability |` tables and the two rows of the `| Axis | Score (0–10) |` tables
(`.ufo/evidence/round-31/contract.json`; `.ufo/evidence/round-31/c1-measure.py` docstring). For each
statement the counter takes the last data row in file order of its table type whose first cell is
the statement id, and compares its parsed values with the values the statement's frozen command
prints at the requested revision. Fenced code and HTML comments do not count. An unparsable row or
an unobservable command output is a mismatch, never a match.

```sh
python3 .ufo/evidence/round-31/c1-measure.py --rev REV --work EMPTY_SCRATCH_DIR
```

The base receipt (`.ufo/evidence/round-31/before/c1-at-base.stdout`) records seven mismatches of
twelve at `36c1d393`: the census row count (44 stated, 92 printed), the runner selftest (80/80 vs
106/106), the regression ledger (6 legs vs 9), the pin-disposition selftest (18/18 vs 19/19), the
evidence-disposition selftest (34/34 vs 66/66), and the depth and calibration scores of the round-1
baseline table (6 and 0 vs 9 and 8). Five matched. A round-17 prose line already marked four
capability counts as dated literals and gave successor counts; three of those successor counts were
stale again at base (runner 95/95, regression 7, evidence-disposition 56/56), so the prose
supersession was itself a standing statement that drifted.

## Preserve the old statement

Correct a stale row by appending a new statement; never edit or delete the old row. The frozen C1
predicate requires the base `SCORECARD.md` to stay a byte prefix and reads the last matching row,
so the old record stays readable and the later row carries the current claim. The new row names its
measured revision, so it is itself a dated claim that the next re-check can confirm or replace.
This append-only rule is an inference from the local predicate, not a claim of S055, S095 or S096.

## Limits

- A matching tally shows only that the selected row values equal the command's parsed output at that
  revision. It is not proof that the capability works in every way its prose describes.
- The check covers the frozen rows and phrase forms only. Other standing numbers in the file (the
  saturation sentence, line cites, receipt descriptions; seat ScoutStatements found four stale ones
  at the freeze) and the three later `| capabilities addition |` tables are outside it.
- Results depend on the environment: the counter runs each command in a fresh clone with the real
  sibling repos symlinked into its work directory (the regression replay reads them; seat
  SentinelCounter found the replay's git use read-only but the symlinks writable in principle), and a
  tool that needs a missing Python module prints SETUP on this host whatever the row says.
- An honest restatement copied from current committed receipts meets the check as well as a fresh
  run does (control CtlReceiptCopy): the check measures agreement, not how the values were obtained.

# A fixture shrinker for a mutant's killing case: 1-minimal by single-unit removal, valid on the pristine gate, and costed in guard runs

Round 50 (claim C2) adds one shrinker, `tools/shrink-case.py`, for one gate pair: the round-43
pre-adoption id guard `tools/staged-id-guard.py` (sha256 `03a796c5…`, never edited) and the round-49
generator's oracle `tools/pbt-staged-id.py` (frozen at `7d3d977f`, sha256 `0cbee392…`). Its input is
the generator's counterexample — the first failing case — and its output is a sub-case of that case
from which no single unit can be removed without losing the kill, with every guard invocation it made
counted. It is the piece the round-49 entry named as missing: "No shrinking: a counterexample is the
first failing case, not a minimal one" (`corpus/knowledge/pbt-generator-pilot.md`, §What this does not
establish). Measured values live in the round's deciding receipt — `deciding-run.sh` writes each
counter's stdout into the `OUTDIR` it is handed — never in this text.

## What the sources state

- **1-minimality is a removal property, not a size.** S271, §I: "It stops when a minimal test case is
  reached, where removing any single input entity would cause the failure to disappear." S024 states
  the same result property for its own reducer: "Its result is 1-minimal, meaning that every character
  contained is required to produce the error". Neither source treats "reduced" as "small": the witness
  is that every remaining entity is load-bearing.
- **The cost is part of the result, and its unit is test runs.** S271, §I: "After 57 tests, the
  original 896-line HTML input is reduced to the minimal failing test case" — one reduction, one run count
  (the Abstract's 139 runs is the case study's total — inference: two reductions summed, 82 + 57; see
  `corpus/knowledge/delta-debugging-minimization-contract.md`). A reduction reported without its run count
  cannot be compared with another reduction; runs are also the unit the lane counts everywhere else.
- **A reduced case must still be a valid input.** S022, Abstract: internal reduction works "internally,
  to the sequence of random choices made during generation", which "significantly mitigates the impact
  of the test-case validity problem, by ensuring that any reduced test case is one that could in
  principle have been generated". The lane's check is the same idea made operational without a
  generator on the other side: the shrunk case must still be answered by the pristine guard exactly as
  the round-49 oracle expects — otherwise it is not an input of this gate at all, and its effect on the
  mutant says nothing.
- **A reducer cannot manufacture an interesting input.** The lane's round-29 F6 attempt ran ddmin over
  a fixture for which no subset was interesting, and kept nothing: "ddmin made 171 oracle tests and
  kept nothing, because no subset kills" (`corpus/knowledge/survivor-fixture-minimization.md`, §What
  happened). Round 49 then supplied exactly what that attempt lacked: a case that violates, found by
  the frozen generator at seed 4949 over 400 cases and dumped with its index.

## What the lane built

- **One shrinker, one gate pair, one starting case per mutant.** `tools/shrink-case.py` takes a case in
  the generator's dump format (`{registry, staged, map}`), a pristine guard and a mutant guard, and
  writes `{case, runs, units_before, units_after}`. The interface is frozen in the round's contract
  (`claims.C2.shrinker_interface`): `--pristine P --mutant M --case CASE.json --out OUT.json`, plus
  `--selftest`; it may import `pbt-staged-id.py` from its own directory; standard library only;
  deterministic; exit 2 with a reason on a setup error. It edits neither guard.
- **Units are the generator's own granularity.** A unit is one registry line, one staged line, or one
  entry of `map['map']` when the case carries a map; every other field of the map document is held
  fixed. The counter counts units the same way and enumerates every single-unit removal from the
  emitted case, so the unit definition is not the shrinker's private choice.
- **Interestingness is the round-49 oracle, through the guards' CLI.** The generator's `check` compares
  a guard run with its own re-implementation of the guard's round-43 rules; `run_guard` writes the
  three inputs and calls the guard as a subprocess. A kill is: `check` returns None on the pristine
  guard (the case is answered as the oracle expects, including a setup refusal with its reason) and
  non-None on the mutant.
- **Method: delta debugging to a fixpoint, with verdict caching.** Drop chunks of decreasing size, try
  one chunk as the new set, refine the granularity, then a single-unit pass to a fixpoint — the last
  pass restates 1-minimality directly rather than relying on the search above it. Verdicts are cached
  by case content, so no case is run twice, and every guard invocation, pristine and mutant, is counted
  into `runs`.
- **Selftest.** `--selftest` runs the search on synthetic interestingness predicates (a sentinel that
  requires one unit, a size floor that leaves a 1-minimal set of three, an unsatisfiable predicate, an
  always-true predicate), a stub CLI end to end, and — when the guard and the generator sit beside the
  tool — the public round-49 panel's M02 edit against the real guard.

## How it is measured, and the control

The frozen counter `.ufo/evidence/round-50/c2/measure.py` (label `C2_R50_PASS`) takes nothing on the
shrinker's word. For each mutant of the 20-case panel — the 12 public round-49 mutants
(`.ufo/evidence/round-49/c2/panel.json`, sha256 `d6dd2cf3…`) and 8 hidden round-50 mutants, whose digest
the contract pins and which the deciding script reads from the revision under test — it finds the
counterexample with the frozen generator (rev `7d3d977f`, seed 4949, 400 cases), hands the case to the
shrinker at the revision under test, and then judges the emitted case itself:

- **sub-case**: registry and staged lines must be subsequences of the original, map entries a subset,
  every other map field equal;
- **kill and 1-minimality**: the counter re-runs the oracle on the pristine and the mutant guard for the
  emitted case, then for every case with exactly one unit removed — each such case must no longer kill.
  This is S271's stopping rule applied at the lane's unit granularity, checked by the measurer, not
  attested by the tool;
- **cost**: both guards are instrumented copies that log every invocation to a `.runs` file; the stated
  `runs` must equal the number of logged invocations, and `units_before`/`units_after` must equal the
  counter's own counts of the original and emitted cases;
- **records and selftest**: `corpus/README.md` carries a line naming F6 and `held (round 50)`, a
  knowledge entry new since base names F6 and cites a mined SOURCES row opened 2026-10-26, and the
  tool's `--selftest` exits 0.

PASS requires at least 19 of the 20 mutants to be ok on every check, with the ok mutants shrinking in
total. The counter's own 9-case selftest drives `measure()` end to end on a fixture repo with four
shrinkers — reference, cost-liar, identity, non-subset — plus an absent shrinker, a failing tool
selftest, missing records, a panel-digest mismatch and an instrumentation check
(`.ufo/evidence/round-50/control/c2-selftest.stdout`: `cases=9 failed=0`); that shape is deliberate,
because round 49's counter selftests never reached `measure()`. The positive control is the counter's own greedy-to-fixpoint reference shrinker: at freeze
bytes it meets the bar on the whole panel, 20/20, units 164 → 43 (`.ufo/evidence/round-50/control/c2-CTL_REF.stdout`,
last line). The panel is therefore reachable, and a plain greedy loop suffices; what this entry adds is
the capability with its stated cost, not a search result.

## What this does not establish

- Units are lines and map entries, not cells. A shrinker cannot cut inside a line — an id, a URL, one
  table cell — so the smallest reducible entity is a whole line or one map entry, and a case cannot be
  reduced to the single cell the mutant actually needs.
- The starting cases are the round-49 generator's tiny cases (small markdown registries and staged
  tables, two to eight rows across the pair). A reduction of a directory fixture, a long log or a
  compiled input is not measured here.
- A greedy-to-fixpoint loop meets the same bar (the positive control above). No claim is made that
  ddmin beats greedy; the logged run count makes such a comparison possible, not concluded.
- F6 names fixture minimization *for survivors*. These mutants are killed by the generator's case, not
  survivors of a fixture battery, and the round-29 B5 survivor stays masked
  (`corpus/knowledge/survivor-fixture-minimization.md:53,57`); the F6 move this entry carries is the
  method on killing cases, B5 is not discharged.
- One lane-owned gate and its 20 mutants. The hidden 8 probe generalisation over mutants found at one
  seed, not over other gates, other seeds, or other unit definitions.
- A kill is oracle agreement, not admission: the pristine side counts as passing when the guard's
  answer matches the oracle, which includes a setup refusal. The counter also cannot tell a 1-minimal
  sub-case a reader can interpret from one that is merely small and still interesting.
- The counter sees the search only through its logged cost and the resulting case; chunk order and
  cache reuse are outside the measurement.
- Under the counter's copy layout only the generator sits beside the shrinker, so the tool's
  real-guard selftest leg is skipped in the measured run (14 cases there, 21 when the guard sits beside
  it). The selftest the counter accepts is the synthetic and stub-CLI part; the real-guard leg is
  evidence outside the counter.

# A flaky verdict can be predicted from recorded history (reported); what a one-run gate verdict is worth is this lane's inference

Two committed snapshots are the whole ground of this entry: the arXiv abstract page of arXiv:2302.09330v2 (S261) and the camera-ready text of Lam, Winter, Astorga, Stodden and Marinov (S262). Both were read through their committed bytes, not fetched live for this draft. Every quotation below was located in the snapshot's folded text, and its whitespace-token count after that fold is given; every number is followed by the line of the committed text file or the page field it came from. Statements about what this lane should do are marked `[INFERENCE]`.

## What the sources state

**Snapshots and visible fields.** S261 is `.ufo/evidence/round-47/coverage/sources/arxiv-2302.09330-abs.html`, 43,549 B, sha256 `2965343ceaac627ccf71f587d3108073c6b45e08b89db3bbe1521a5716e14bc6`, fetched 2026-10-25. Its metadata cells read `arXiv:2302.09330v2 [cs.SE]`, `Submitted on 18 Feb 2023 (v1), last revised 18 Mar 2023 (this version, v2)`, `12 pages, to be published in the Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST 2023)`, and the DataCite DOI `10.48550/arXiv.2302.09330`; the title is *Practical Flaky Test Prediction using Common Code Evolution and Test History Data* (Martin Gruber, Michael Heine, Norbert Oster, Michael Philippsen, Gordon Fraser).

S262 is the camera-ready PDF `.ufo/evidence/round-47/coverage/sources/lam-2020-reruns.pdf`, 11 pages, 565,435 B, sha256 `0b88045817f146db3eb26d305c864291010e5c083aa8d5cac480be3c5350895d`, and its committed text snapshot `.ufo/evidence/round-47/coverage/sources/lam-2020-reruns.txt`, produced with pdftotext 26.08.0 `-layout`, 81,725 B, sha256 `bf52c9089e331f18bb65c3c03449de070723c7ec52725c0e6dc84ca249b025b9`. The text is two columns per page, so a sentence that crosses the column gutter is interleaved in the extracted text: every quotation below is a fragment wholly inside one column, and `lam-2020-reruns.txt:NNN` names the line it occupies. The text carries `©2020 IEEE` (`:63`) and contains no venue string; the PDF metadata names TeX and pdfTeX 1.40.20 only, so this snapshot does not state where the paper was published and this entry does not claim it.

### S261 — flakiness predicted from outcomes, durations and code history, with no added reruns

The motivation is a loss of trust, not a taxonomy: "Non-deterministically behaving test cases cause developers to lose trust in their regression test suites" (14 tokens) and "Detecting flaky tests is therefore a crucial task in maintaining code quality" (12 tokens) — §Abstract.

The obstacle the paper is built against is deployment inside industry: "their reliance on instrumentation, test reruns, or language-specific artifacts was inhibitive" (11 tokens) — §Abstract. What the authors do instead: "we therefore investigate the prediction of flaky tests without such requirements on the underlying programming language, CI, build or test execution framework" (22 tokens) — §Abstract.

The inputs are cheap and already recorded: "we rely only on the most commonly available artifacts, namely the tests' outcomes and durations" (15 tokens), and "our approach does not require additional reruns, since it gathers this data from existing test executions" (16 tokens) — both §Abstract.

The evaluation is one system, with a balanced set: "evaluated their performance on a large-scale industrial software system" (9 tokens) and "we collected a data set of 100 flaky and 100 non-flaky test- and code-histories" (14 tokens) — §Abstract. The headline: "The best model was able to achieve an F1-score of 95.5% using only 3 features" (15 tokens) — §Abstract — with the three named in the same abstract as "the number of changes to source files in the last 54 days" (12 tokens) plus the flip rate and the changed-file count of the most recent pull request.

### S262 — what reruns buy, and how little a single order says

The paper's flaky label is a rerun outcome, not a static property: "we label tests as flaky if our runs have both pass and fail" (13 tokens) — §I, `lam-2020-reruns.txt:29`. The measurement is heavy: "we run each test suite exactly 4000 times, potentially" (9 tokens, `:91`), "running every test suite 4000 times in 40 batches, and every" (11 tokens, `:591`), and "we again run it 4000 times in isolation" (8 tokens, `:593`). Its population is Java and Maven: "we perform our empirical evaluation on Java projects that rely" (10 tokens, `:25`), with "A threat to validity is that our study uses only 26 modules" (12 tokens, `:582`) and 23 Maven-based Java projects (`:583`).

The guidance block, §I `:114-115`, prices the check: "one can use ≤ 5 reruns (50% less than Google's default ten" (12 tokens) "reruns [6]) and still check correctly ≥ 82% of the time." (11 tokens). The detection guidance is about order, not repetition: "RQ2 & RQ3: To detect flaky tests, one should run tests in" (12 tokens) "orders with fewer times each, rather than fewer orders with" (10 tokens) — §I `:116-118`.

Order matters because the old category was wrong: "In contrast to OD tests that fail deterministically" (8 tokens, `:48`), "the majority of NOD tests are actually" (7 tokens, `:122`) NDOD, and of the manually inspected set, "found 7 OD, 14 NDOD, 4 NDOI, and 3 more NOD that are" (13 tokens) difficult to classify — §VI, `:459-460` after "In sum, we inspected 28 tests and" (7 tokens, `:459`).

Reproducing a suite failure in isolation is not free: "ISO did not detect 57 tests by itself" (8 tokens, §V-C, `:438`), and "Guideline: We find that 53% of flaky tests detected in TSO" (11 tokens, `:452`) "runs are not detected in ISO runs." The burst length needed is longer in isolation: "we observe that TSO reaches 82% for a maximal" (9 tokens, `:439`) burst length of 2, while "for a maximal burst length of 5 test failures instead" (10 tokens, `:442`) is what ISO needs to reach the same share.

The suite-level price is measured, not estimated: "developers encounter TSR failures between <0.1%" (6 tokens, §V-D, `:479`) and 50% (`:480`), and "TSR failure in 5.4% of TSRs." ## What this means for fixture craft

Everything in this section is `[INFERENCE]`: neither snapshot measures this lane, its gates, its controls or its counters.

- **A single run is a sample, and the sources price the second one.** S262 states what a small budget buys: at most five reruns still check correctly at least 82% of the time on their data (`:114-115`), and S261 states that a model over recorded history needs no added reruns at all (§Abstract). `[INFERENCE]` A lane that wants a flaky-aware verdict therefore has exactly two honest routes: pay reruns at verdict time, or consume a history that already exists. The evidence this round's claims rest on is one observation per statement-profile and one selftest invocation per mutant — the C1 surface compares the (line, exit) a statement prints under six profiles (`.ufo/evidence/round-47/contract.json` C1 `surface`) and C2's kill rule is a predicate on one selftest invocation's exit status and its `FAIL ` line (same file, C2 `statement`) — so no flaky-aware claim can be read off those observations without a repeat or a history.
- **Order diversity and repetition answer different questions.** S262's detection advice is more orders with fewer runs each, not fewer orders with many runs each (`:116-118`), because the paper reports that the majority of NOD tests are actually NDOD, i.e. order-dependent (`:122`, `:459-460`). `[INFERENCE]` The F3 control (`corpus/README.md` F3 row: N ≥ 3 byte-identical controls) is the other question — whether one exact argv prints the same stream — so the 82% figure must not be transferred to it, and three identical controls do not constitute evidence about detection.
- **A verdict that reads the clock is partly a verdict about the host.** S262's example test is flaky only because runs cross a 1500 ms limit, and its failure rate is 39.1% in isolation against 10.9% in its suite, 0%–20.1% by order (`:148-167`). `[INFERENCE]` Any gate that scores a timeout, or compares durations, is measuring load as well as code; the frozen C2 kill rule already declines that class — a crash or a timeout is not a kill (`.ufo/evidence/round-47/contract.json` C2 `statement`) — which keeps a load-sensitive outcome out of this round's mutation score. The same inference argues against a gate that reads a wall-clock budget without recording it.
- **The 82% has a narrow referent.** The quoted sentence is about checking whether a failure is due to flakiness (§I `:113-115`), on 26 modules from 23 projects (`:582-583`), with their flaky definition being both outcomes across reruns (`:29`). `[INFERENCE]` It is not a bound on verdict correctness, not a promise that five reruns settle a mutation score, and not measured on bash or JavaScript CLI suites.
- **Prediction features are code-history features of a different subject.** S261's features are flip rate, source churn over 54 days and the size of the latest pull request (§Abstract) for the test cases of one industrial system. `[INFERENCE]` Nothing in the abstract supports computing them for this lane's statements and gates, and the abstract reports no transfer experiment.

The mechanism is three triggers, stated from the owner's side, plus one mechanical pin read that says which trigger fired. It governs the six measured rows above; a first sweep of an unmeasured §3 gate is not a re-sweep.

*The pin read (one command set per case, run at the boundary — the executed instance follows):*

    sha256sum <gate-file>                                # vs the case row's recorded pin
    git -C <owner-repo> show HEAD:<path> | sha256sum     # is the recorded revision the HEAD blob?
    git -C <owner-repo> status --porcelain -- <path>     # working tree vs HEAD

*Readings.* **current** — recorded pin = live file = HEAD blob, tree clean (the row's pin still names the object; a re-sweep is a fresh reading, not a repair). **stale** — the recorded revision is an ancestor of the live gate; the substrate moved after the sweep (trigger 3). **drift** — the working tree differs from its HEAD (a writer is on the gate; wait for the commit, then re-pin). The read is hygiene and a trigger reading, not a replay guard: the harness's legs materialize from git blobs (`git show <rev>:<path>`), so a drifted tree cannot move a materialized leg (`reports/r7-aud-t7.md` §2–§3).

# The gate's exit map and the registry rows that pin it (round 57)

## Why a gate needs executed rows beyond its selftest

`receipt-revision-gate.py --selftest` builds its own repository under `TMPDIR` and proves
that each code fires on that fixture. It does not prove that the command the lane writes
down runs (relative `--lane .`, a relative receipt path, cwd at the lane root), that the
receipt bytes the lane committed still give the recorded verdict, or that the entry resolves
at a revision. A registry row is the executed form of those three: `registry-check.py --rev REV`
clones the revision, runs the row's `argv` from the clone root, and holds the row only when
the exit equals `expect.exit` and every `stdout_contains` needle appears. Measured at base,
where the lane has no `tools/fixtures/receipt-gate/` tree (`lane-demo.stdout`), the staged
accept row's command gives `RECEIPT_MISSING` (rc 3) from the lane while the selftest reads
`GATE_SELFTEST: 19/19 pass` (rc 0). A row goes red on that; the selftest does not.

## 4. Evidence discipline — five shared habits

**[OBS]** Measured across all six; each is a repeatable pattern, not a one-off.

1. **A verdict line is a summary, and a summary must be last.**
   `claim-ledger.sh:26-28` states the rule: a claim passes only when the exit
   code equals the expected one **and** the expected ERE matches the *last
   non-empty output line*. `claim-ledger.sh:423` emits
   `FAIL <id> reason=verdict-not-final exit=<rc>` for the case that prints a
   verdict-shaped string and then fails. **[INF]** this is the single most
   portable idea in the set — a check that greps anywhere in stdout can be
   satisfied by a warning line.
2. **Verdicts carry their counts, not just their name.**
   `SURFACE_CENSUS: DRIFT (diverged=… gone=… …)` (`surface-census.sh:865`),
   `DRIFT_PINS: DRIFT (files_ok=… files_bad=… symbols_ok=… symbols_bad=…)`
   (`drift-pins.sh:253`), `OP_REF_PROBE: DRIFT (checks=… failed=… …)`
   (`op-ref-probe.sh:442`), `ADJACENCY_SCOPE: DEFECT (…)` with 25 named counters
   (`scope-gate.sh:659`, `CLEAN` at `:657`; observed run in §6), and
   `CLAIM_LEDGER: FAIL (claims=… failed=… deferred=…)` (`claim-ledger.sh:950-951`,
   `CLAIM_LEDGER: POLICY` at `:946`). A reader can tell *how much*
   drifted without re-running.
3. **Count-only pins where a name would be the leak.**
   `drift-pins.sh:14-16` — a `COUNT` verdict form (`<path>:#<pin>->#<actual>`)
   exists precisely because naming the matched text would leak; `:19-24` — the
   `op.env` row is pinned by mode + lines only, sha field `-`, since a content
   hash of a secret-bearing file is an offline guessing oracle.
   `scope-gate.sh:19-20` — breadth pins are count-only, so no private child-name
   manifest is committed (`# breadth <dir>  children=<N>  declared=<M>` is the
   whole schema, `scope-gate.sh:25`). **[INF]** this is the clean answer to "pin
   the host without publishing the host".
4. **Abstention is declared, counted, and exit-neutral.**
   `scope-gate.sh:52-55` — `unresolved` / `contested` are *declared* classes
   printed in the summary; a legitimately absent runtime row abstains from R9
   (`ADJACENCY_ABSTAIN: rows=N`); but a path that exists and cannot be resolved
   is `UNVERIFIED` and **fails closed** (`scope-gate.sh:1077` selftest asserts
   this). `surface-census.sh:37-38` — exit 0 is returned even when the only
   non-OK lines are `ABSENT`/`SKIP`.
   `claim-ledger.sh:397-398` — a `[substrate]`-tagged row prints
   `DEFER <id> reason=substrate-absent` and does not fail.
   **[INF]** the guard that keeps this from becoming a blanket excuse is
   `claim-ledger.sh:136-137`: a row that defers while the substrate is *present*
   is a genuine run, and the selftest proves both paths (`:1313-1315`).
5. **Secret hygiene is stated in the header as a prohibition, not a hope.**
   `surface-census.sh:40`, `drift-pins.sh:21`, `checklist-run.sh:41`,
   `scope-gate.sh:58`, `claim-ledger.sh:84`. Notably `claim-ledger.sh:85-86`:
   the gate *never echoes a claim's output* — only the verdict line is matched,
   never printed, because a claim could read a private file.

## 9. Reusable pattern (candidate — for the tameshi method, not a claim on kagi)

**[INF]** The six gates share an eleven-item shape that looks portable. Stated as
a checklist, with the kagi anchor that evidences each item, and explicitly *not*
claimed as a fleet generalisation — per `tameshi-shokunin/PROVINCE.md`, a pattern
is admitted from evidence in **two** independent lanes:

1. Three-valued exit lattice, same meaning everywhere (§3 table).
2. POLICY class separate from SETUP, both exit 2, both *before* the effect.
3. Malformed committed data is not a verdict (§3.2) — note the five gates that
   still disagree on which exit code this earns.
4. Last-non-empty-line rule for any verdict-shaped expectation
   (`claim-ledger.sh:53-56`).
5. Zero-work is a setup error, never a clean run (`claim-ledger.sh:757`, `:762`).
6. Abstentions named, counted, exit-neutral, and pinned by a both-paths selftest
   (`claim-ledger.sh:136-137`, `:1313-1315`).
7. Count-only pins wherever a name would leak (§4.3).
8. Scratch-tree selftest that *fires* every rule, run as the proof
   (§2; the case counts are the evidence). **Amended after F-2 (§6b):** "every
   rule" is an aspiration, not a property — measure the refusal paths against the
   asserted ones before repeating the claim.
9. A mutation mode that attacks the gate itself (`scope-gate.sh:669`, `--falsify`).
10. Secret hygiene stated as a prohibition in the header (§4.5).
11. Revision stamps so a reader can name the artefact they read (§5.3).

**[INF]** Items 4, 5, 6 and 7 are the ones with a *measured cost of absence*
recorded in kagi's own history: item 4's absence let a verdict-shaped-then-failed
command pass; item 5's absence would make an empty audit look green; item 7's
absence would either leak or forbid pinning at all. Items 1–3 are cheap and
structural. The candidate is a tameshi hypothesis until a second lane's gates
show the same shape.

## 8. Inference (I)

1. I: the "every declared kind fires" meta-checks are arm-coverage detectors,
   not mutation controls — they prove each branch is *reached*, not that a
   wrong implementation would be *caught* (e.g. claims-check 827 named the one
   case where a kind-blind mutant would be caught).
2. I: cite-check's hermetic group is the weakest of the six on
   self-checking axes (no arm-coverage meta-check, no mutation arm, substring
   verdict asserts); its compensating strength is repair-regression case names
   citing rounds 13/23/25-29 (e.g. 139, 161, 2034, 1711-1829).
3. I: the hermetic counts are loop-sensitive (proxy 71 literal sites → 102
   cases; claims 35 → 39; kimi 41 → 43), so "case count" in any report must
   name the executed summary line, not a source grep.

# A golden comparison has three outcomes, and the path that writes the expected value is a flagged path

## What the sources state

- POSIX `diff` returns three exit values, not two: `0` "No differences were found", `1`
  "Differences were found", and greater than `1` "An error occurred" (S105, §EXIT STATUS,
  lines 564-574). The same specification names `LANG` (162), `LC_ALL` (166) and `TZ` (191)
  among the environment variables that affect the execution of `diff` (§ENVIRONMENT
  VARIABLES).
- `google/golden`'s `Compare` returns the unified diff when the actual value differs from
  the golden file, and the write path that overwrites the golden file is gated on the
  `-update_golden` flag (S106, `Compare` doc comment, lines 72-73; `shouldUpdateGolden()`
  branch, line 78).

## The three-outcome rule

A golden comparison is classified into exactly three outcomes, and the third one is the one
a two-outcome harness drops:

| outcome | condition | what it means for a fixture |
|---|---|---|
| match | the comparison ran and found no differences | the fixture's expectation holds; this is the only outcome that may be called green |
| differ | the comparison ran and found differences | the artifact under test changed, or the expected value is stale |
| error | the comparison could not be made (exit > 1, or a required file is absent) | nothing was compared; the fixture proved nothing and must not be recorded as a red |

Two consequences for the lane's own craft:

1. **A comparison that could not be made is not a failure of the code under test.** S105's
   `>1` class is an error class, distinct from the difference class. A harness that
   collapses "differ" and "error" into one verdict cannot tell "the code changed" from
   "the comparison never happened". The lane's fixture for this rule classifies three
   outcomes and asserts the error class explicitly
   (`tools/golden-verdict.py --selftest`; counter `.ufo/evidence/round-38/golden/measure.py`).
2. **The write path must be explicit.** In S106 the overwrite path sits behind
   `-update_golden`; the normal path only reads and compares. Inference from S106's
   structure: a golden fixture whose expected value can be rewritten without a
   distinguishable flag has no fail-closed arm for that write. The lane's own open F4
   measurement — "update paths that write expected values without an explicit flag:
   unmeasured -> counted per surveyed gate" — is **not** measured here; the lane's
   surveyed gates were not audited in this round.

## Boundary of this entry

- The exit-status class is POSIX `diff`'s. `cmp`, `git diff --exit-code` and other
  comparators have their own lattices and are not covered by this entry.
- The environment-variable list names what the specification says affects `diff`; it does
  not by itself make any comparison byte-reproducible under an unnormalized environment.
- Nothing here measures the lane's own gates, and no claim is made that the lane's
  fixtures are golden-comparison fixtures today.

## 1. A guard is covered only when two legs hold

Rule. A guard G is covered by its owning `--selftest` only when both hold at the same rev:

- (a) pristine green: the unmodified selftest exits 0. A nonzero pristine exit is could-not-evaluate (exit 2), never "closed".
- (b) kill: the selftest exits nonzero when G's single-occurrence guard text is removed (the mutant applied to a copy).

Why (a). Without it, a broken selftest makes every mutant read as killed. K04 found that contract A never required a green pristine run, so an always-failing collector would read all three probes as closed [w1/K04TracePromotion.md:65-71]. X03 implements the fix: each guard-removal probe runs its owning pristine selftest first, and nonzero is an evaluation error [w1/X03DefectProbes.md:29].

Why not existence. A mutant that survives is not behavioural coverage. K01 states that a guard-removal probe measures mutant sensitivity, not that the guard works [w1/K01ProbeRulerGaming.md:14-20]. The round-17 lesson says the same: code existence is not behavioural coverage [lesson §7 item 3, `corpus/lessons/round-17-verifier-spotcheck.md:428-432`].

Meta-cheat. A selftest case that hashes or greps its own source kills every P01–P07 mutant with no behavioural coverage [w1/K01ProbeRulerGaming.md:83-89]. A kill that comes from an unrelated case tripped by a side effect of the mutant is incidental [w1/K01ProbeRulerGaming.md:91-96]. Detection: the probe prints the failing case names, and a case that reads the tool's own bytes does not count.

## 2. jj colocation: HEAD is `@-` and can differ from the branch tip

Fact. In a colocated repository, Git HEAD is the working-copy parent `@-`. It is not the branch tip when a commit is made without moving the bookmark [src: S061 row, `corpus/SOURCES.md:70`; w1/C02MoriJjPatterns.md:35-43]. Measured on jj 0.45.1 and git 2.56.0 in /tmp [w1/C02MoriJjPatterns.md:31].

- `jj git init --colocate` alone leaves HEAD attached at the branch tip, so it does not create the divergence [w1/C03FleetJjPractice.md:40, :47].
- `jj new` moves HEAD to the previous working-copy commit. Commit ids diverge but trees do not, so a byte check cannot see it [w1/C03FleetJjPractice.md:41, :48].
- `jj commit` of a content change, before `bookmark set`, moves HEAD to the new `@-`. The live bytes match `HEAD:` and differ from `refs/heads/<branch>:` [w1/C03FleetJjPractice.md:49].
- After `bookmark set`, HEAD equals the branch tip and stays detached [w1/C03FleetJjPractice.md:43, :50].

S074 bears on step 3. `git symbolic-ref HEAD` names the branch only when HEAD is attached. With `-q`, a detached HEAD exits 1 silently and any other error exits 128. A resolver must branch on exit 1 as "detached", not as a read failure [src: S074, quotes A–C].

## 4. Process escape: setsid and setpgid leave the group

Fact. `setsid()` makes the caller the only process in a new process group and a new session [src: S069, quote "The calling process will be the only process in the new process group and in the new session."]. A group-directed signal to the old group therefore does not reach it. That consequence is inference from the new group ID; `killpg` is not named on the man page [src: S069, Gate note]. `setsid` fails with EPERM for a process group leader, so an escaping process must fork first [src: S069, §ERRORS].

Subreaper rule. An orphaned process is reparented to the nearest living ancestor subreaper. Quote: "When a process becomes orphaned (i.e., its immediate parent terminates), then that process will be reparented to the nearest still living ancestor subreaper." [src: S068, PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER(2const) §DESCRIPTION]. This is the rule the cleanup walk relies on: an escapee that double-forks stays a descendant of the checker while the checker is the nearest subreaper.

Base code. `_kill_group` signals only `os.getpgid(proc.pid)` with `os.killpg` at `[lane:tools/registry-check.py:306-322]`. The row starts with `start_new_session=True` at `[lane:tools/registry-check.py:375]`. After timeout the code calls `proc.communicate()` with no timeout at `[lane:tools/registry-check.py:387]` [w1/S10TimeoutEscapeSweep.md:42-43].

Observed. `setsid` escapes a group kill (`survivors=[5]`), and so does a plain `os.setpgid(0,0)` [receipt:P10; w1/X03DefectProbes.md:47]. Both checkers returned `got=timeout`. A `setsid` escapee holding the row's pipe held the monitor for 6037 ms with `timeout_s: 1` [w1/S10TimeoutEscapeSweep.md:18-20]. A row that exits before its timeout can leave a daemonised child alive while the row reports held [w1/S10TimeoutEscapeSweep.md:14-16].

PID reuse. `proc.pid` is a bare number after the leader exits. If it is reused before `os.getpgid` runs, `killpg` can signal an unrelated group [w1/N02KillScopeSafety.md:21].

Required design, from the reviews.

- Set `PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER` before each row. Failure is "unavailable", not a fallback to group-only cleanup [w1/N02KillScopeSafety.md:27; w1/X05RegistryCheck.md:7, :43]. The reparenting rule is S068 above.
- Walk `/proc` ancestry by process leaders. Parse `stat` after the last `)`. Keep identities `(pid, starttime)`, not UID, session or group [w1/N02KillScopeSafety.md:28].
- Revalidate starttime after `pidfd_open`, then signal through the pidfd. Never a later numeric `kill` [w1/N02KillScopeSafety.md:29; w1/X05RegistryCheck.md:7].
- Drain bounded: bound `communicate` and the final wait. Completion is "no visible row descendant", not "pipe closed" [w1/X05RegistryCheck.md:7; w1/V02TimeoutIntent.md:33].
- A cgroup with `cgroup.kill` is the stronger guarantee against PID reuse and parentage escape. If it is unavailable, state the weaker guarantee [w1/N02KillScopeSafety.md:32].

Residual limits. A descendant that changes UID is not signalable by an unprivileged monitor (EPERM) [w1/V02TimeoutIntent.md:31]. A same-tick PID reuse can race before the pidfd opens, because starttime has tick granularity [w1/X05RegistryCheck.md:43]. A double-forked descendant cannot leave an active subreaper's tree [w1/X05RegistryCheck.md:43].

PENDING. The base is process-group-only cleanup. The subreaper and walk exist only in the staged X05 source, and its falsifier table is staged evidence, not landed evidence.

# Hermetic environment differential — vary one input, keep the repeat control

## What the experiment asks

Does a pinned selftest's **raw exit/stdout/stderr tuple** change when the
launcher changes a finite, declared environmental input? A passing result
is not proof that the target accesses only declared resources. Bazel S028's
hermeticity definition is stronger than this experiment: declared inputs,
not merely seven observed environmental configurations.

S079 demonstrates explicit TZ as a way to control timezone-dependent tool
output. It supports the controlled-TZ profile, not the claim that every gate
will honor TZ or that every source of nondeterminism has been removed.

## Frozen population and recipes

The nine repo/revision/path pins are in
`.ufo/evidence/round-21/c2-contract.json`; eight SHA-256 pins are the existing
mutation-ledger pins, and the ninth fixes the tameshi runner at08175c6.
No target or sibling repository is modified. The tool materializes each
blob, verifies any declared SHA, and starts the selftest in a fresh bwrap
scratch with a read-only root, private writable `/tmp/w`, and no network.
The interpreter and filesystem outside scratch remain host resources;
this does not isolate kernel/runtime versions or provide a full VM.

| Profile | Environment delta |
|---|---|
| host | inherit invoking environment except all GIT_* variables |
| clean | empty environment plus PATH, private HOME/TMPDIR, LANG=C, LC_ALL=C, TZ=UTC |
| clean_repeat | the same clean values, a second execution in fresh scratch |
| tz | clean, changing only TZ to Pacific/Chatham |
| locale | clean, changing LANG/LC_ALL to en_US.UTF-8 |
| home | clean, changing HOME to /nonexistent |
| columns | clean, adding COLUMNS=20, LINES=5, TERM=dumb |

PATH remains a declared host dependency, not a pinned executable identity.
The locale profile requires that locale on the observation host; missing
locale behavior is not silently normalized. Host inheritance is not an
inventory of all possible environmental values. No environment dump or
credential values are persisted in the receipt.

## Decision table

| Observation | Classification | Allowed conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| Missing process/bwrap, timeout, missing/mismatched blob, or red clean control | unavailable | No completed comparison; do not count this surface |
| clean raw tuple differs from clean_repeat | nondeterministic | The raw observation is not repeat-identical; do not attribute profile differences to one environment variable |
| repeat-identical clean; every profile tuple equals clean | invariant | No difference observed in this seven-profile sample |
| repeat-identical clean; one or more other profiles differ | env-sensitive | Name exactly the differing profiles; diagnose their output and target source before claiming cause |

Raw streams are SHA-256 hashed without replacing paths or times
(`normalization: none`). Timings are recorded but are not part of the tuple.
No semantic equivalence is inferred from matching exits alone.

## Executed result

Counting the initial committed-receipt candidate's records:
`python3 -c 'import json,collections; d=json.load(open(".ufo/evidence/round-21/f5/receipt-initial.json")); print(collections.Counter(s["classification"] for s in d["surfaces"]))'`
observed eight invariant and one nondeterministic (2026-10-21); all nine

| tameshi-runner | invariant |
| js-kimi-census | invariant |
| bash-surface-census | invariant |
| bash-tsukuroi-census | invariant |
| bash-mado-verify | invariant |

## Reuse boundary

A receipt is reproducible evidence of what was recorded, not authenticated
proof that an arbitrary producer executed it. The frozen counter's metadata
checks cannot detect a fabricated, internally consistent profile receipt;
independent executions remain necessary. New pins, extra profiles, different
runtime versions or output normalization require a new observation with a
separately named population. Do not silently expand the frozen ruler.

# Pin match is not a reuse licence: six-leg content disposition vs a fresh re-sweep

Scope: this entry supports one bounded method step — how a *content* disposition
of the six recorded legs must be read. It does not adopt incremental mutation
testing, does not re-measure any leg, and does not claim the pattern general
across lanes.

## 1. Sources, located (O)

**S003 §Incremental mode.** The page states its reuse predicate as two
conditions (quoted verbatim apart from joining the bullets; the quote marks
around `"Killed"` are as served in the page's HTML):

> Reuse is possible when: A mutant was "Killed"; the culprit test still exists, and it didn't change. A mutant was not "Killed"; no new test covers it, and no tests changed.

and names the comparison it actually makes:

> StrykerJS will do a git-like diff of your code and test files to the previous version it finds in the incremental report file in order to match the mutants and tests to the current version of the code.

The dry run is not skipped:

> The dry run remains required; as it discovers tests, mutation coverage per test, and ensures Stryker runs successfully when no mutant is active.

**S003 §Limitations.** The declared blind spots, verbatim:

> Stryker will not detect any changes you've made in files other than mutated files and test files.

> Any other changes to your environment are not detected, such as updates to other files, updated (dev) dependencies, changes to environment variables, changes to .snap files, readme files, etc.

> Static mutants don't have test coverage; thus, Stryker won't detect test changes for them.

Its runner-support table adds that a command-style runner detects nothing about
tests: "All test details are unknown incremental mode will only detect changes in
mutants, not their tests." (page wording as printed). `--force` is the page's
escape hatch: "With these limitations in mind, you can probably imagine a
scenario where you want to force specific mutants to run while using incremental
mode." It reruns "all mutants in scope, regardless of the incremental file."
The causal reading that it exists *because* detection is incomplete is [I]; the
page does not state a reason.

**S041 §Incremental analysis.** PIT calls the feature experimental and frames
reuse as inference:

> PIT will track changes to the code and tests and store the results from previous runs. It will then use this information to avoid re-running analysis when the results can be logically inferred.

Its skip rules vary by item: rule 1 conditions on the class, rule 2 on the class
and the killing test, rule 3 on the covering tests:

> If a mutation was killed in the last run and neither the class under test or the killing test has changed, then it can be assumed that this mutation is still killed.

> If a mutation survived in the last run, no new tests cover it, and none of the covering tests have changed, then it must still survive.

It then bounds its own claims:

> With the exception of 4), all these optimisations introduce a degree of potential error into the analysis.

Rule 4) is a *prioritisation*, not a reuse skip: a previously killed mutant
whose class or killing test changed "should therefore be prioritised above
others" (since 1.14.4); the pronoun's referent is left as written. Rule 5) is
"not yet implemented". So the live reuse skips are 1)–3), and PIT attributes
potential error to them. **S047 records this precision correction**: item 4 is
a prioritisation rather than a reuse skip, item 5 is only proposed, and the
potential-error sentence covers the optimisations rather than solely live
result-reuse skips. S041's earlier "all but one of its reuse optimisations"
cell is superseded by S047; the original row is retained. The dependency
limitation is explicit:

> The main issue is that class behaviour is defined not only by its bytecode, but also by its dependencies (i.e the classes it interacts with and the graph of classes that they interact with). PIT will only consider the strongest of these dependencies - changes to super classes and outer classes, when deciding if a class's behaviour might have changed.

> So the incremental feature is based on the assumption that it will be relatively rare for changes in the dependencies of a class to change the status of a mutation. Although this assumption seems reasonable, it is currently unproven.

The unimplemented meta-mutant rule carries a further unquantified risk, and
history provenance is the operator's job: with different history locations
"you will need to implement some mechanism to swap the values between runs".

Version state, recorded not smoothed: S003 says only "Available since Stryker
6.2"; S041 and S047 state no PIT version. Both are vendor documentation for
their own tools, and neither discusses content hashes or a gate-file pin.

## 2. What the sources license (O)

- Both tools reuse only under an **unchanged-inputs** predicate, with different
  units: S003 keeps a verdict when the mutant and its tests are unchanged (or
  no new test covers it); PIT keeps the infinite-loop verdict on an unchanged
  class, a killed verdict on an unchanged class and killing test, and a
  survivor on unchanged covering tests.
- Both declare their change detection incomplete. S003 lists environment,
  dependencies, `.snap` files and non-mutated/non-test files as undetected;
  PIT states its optimisations introduce "potential error", considers only the
  strongest class dependencies, and calls the underlying assumption "unproven".
- S047 supersedes S041's wider summary: PIT presents the feature as
  experimental, its dependency assumption is unproven, item 4 is a
  prioritisation exception, and item 5 is not implemented. Nothing there is a
  general reuse guarantee.
- Neither document discusses a content hash, a pin, or a gate artifact. Their
  reuse unit is source/test change against a stored report — not a hash of the
  tool or gate being run.

## 3. The lane's pin object is coarser than either reuse predicate (I)

The runner records, per leg, one blob path, one revision and one sha256
(`tools/mutate-and-run.sh:81-83, 540-553`). A replay materializes
`git show <rev>:<path>` and refuses on any pin mismatch — "a missing
repo/rev/blob or a pin mismatch is a SETUP refusal, never a pass"
(`:99-108`); the `REGRESSION_PIN` line reports exactly that git source and
pinned sha256 (`:119-120`, `:959`). The command that then runs is
`node "$MUTANT" --selftest` or `bash "$MUTANT" --selftest` over the
materialized copy (`:1113-1140`).

The lane's own reading vocabulary is narrower still: a **current** pin means
"recorded pin = live file = HEAD blob, tree clean"; the read is "hygiene and a
trigger reading, not a replay guard" (`fleet-kill-rate-ledger.md` §ER-3).
**stale** and **drift** are the other two readings.

From these observations:

1. [I] Byte identity of the pinned gate file is necessary to even consider
   reusing its recorded verdict table, but it cannot satisfy either source's
   reuse predicate. S003 requires the mutant and its tests to be unchanged
   (or no new covering test); PIT requires the class and the killing/covering
   tests unchanged. The pin names one file. It carries no mutant inventory, no
   test identity, no covering relation, and no dependency closure.
2. [I] The unpinned closure is exactly what both sources name as their blind
   spot: environment variables, (dev) dependencies, sibling files, snapshot
   files, and the runner plugin's test-location support (S003); class
   dependencies beyond super/outer classes (S041). The leg invocation's
   toolchain and any sibling file its selftest reads are outside the pin.
3. [I] Therefore `result_reuse: not_established` is the only defensible reuse
   value for a content-only probe of these six legs. This is a **lane
   inference** from the dependency/environment blind spots S003 and S047 name,
   plus the pin's scope — not a sentence either document writes about pins, and
   not a measured outcome.
4. [O] A replay is not reuse. The harness's exact-band expectation — "0 verdict
   flips … killed-delta 0 … control green, MUTATE_RESTORE: OK"
   (`tools/mutate-and-run.sh:109-114`) — describes a re-execution at the
   recorded pin. It says nothing about what a stored table may be assumed to
   mean on a later, unexecuted run.
5. [O] Byte identity is over file contents only. The runner mirrors the git
   mode because a `100755` blob is required for a self-exec suite
   (`tools/mutate-and-run.sh:104-106`), and round 10 measured a SETUP when the
   materialized copy at the recorded pin lacked the exec bit
   (`plans/round-10-record-draft.md:84-88`). A content status that hashes
   worktree bytes therefore does not even establish that the artifact can run.

## 4. Six-leg content disposition vs a fresh re-sweep (O tameshi; I)

The six recorded legs are tameshi's own-work ground (S031); the runner defines
