**A content disposition is a read-only classification.** Per leg it records the
recorded pin, the current committed blob, the current worktree content and a
status (unchanged / changed / unavailable), plus the reuse field fixed at
`not_established` by §3. It executes no leg, produces no control, no restore
proof, no table and no rate. Its whole product is "do the recorded bytes still
name the object in front of us".

**A fresh re-sweep is an execution.** It names the revision it measures, runs
the suite and a control, applies a single-edit spec whose expectations were
registered before the run, and lands a new row; the ledger's three triggers are
owner hardening, suite changes and substrate drift
(`fleet-kill-rate-ledger.md:306-310`). It is the only artifact that can produce
a new kill-rate.

The two differ in kind, not degree. A disposition row reading `unchanged`
neither re-verifies the recorded table nor authorizes its reuse. [I] A `current`
reading is not itself a re-sweep request: the ledger says a current pin means
"a re-sweep is a fresh reading, not a repair". [I] Because the unpinned
closure can always differ, no content disposition class implies safe reuse;
conversely, `changed`/`unavailable` only says the recorded table is bound to
bytes that are no longer here, which still is not a new measurement. A
`changed` row is the ER-3 trigger-3 condition (substrate drift): a request to
re-pin and re-sweep, never a successor measurement.

**No new kill-rate and no seventh case.** The recorded expectations above are
the six legs' tables; this entry adds no leg, reruns none, and revises no rate.
A prior executed six-row pin read exists as a historical receipt —
`LEDGER: 6 cases in; target current=4 stale=2 drift=0` at 2026-10-14T19:58Z,
rows 3/4 `stale` (`fleet-kill-rate-ledger.md` §ER-4) — and bounds nothing about
current content.

# Cold-read credit must be keyed to the inputs a read ran against

Scope: one method step for this lane's SKILL.md cold-read ledger — when a
recorded read still earns credit for a bucket. It does not make a trace a
sandbox, does not re-read anything by itself, and does not claim the page is
correct.

## 1. The observed hole (O)

Round 16 credited each SKILL.md bucket by the sha256 of its section text
(`.ufo/evidence/round-16/measure.py`, `coldread()`), plus a verdict and a
command count. The bucket `## Effective expectation reconciliation — round 14`
was read once (CR26) with `tools/mutate-and-run.sh` at `75ed934d…`; the
round's own runner edits moved it to `0673d2e5…`. The section bytes did not
change, so it stayed credited, while its recipe now exited 2
`expected_input_digest_mismatch`. The round-16 measure reported 54/54 and
score 8 at `98bea7d` (`.ufo/waves/round-17/w1/S08RunR16Probes.md`). A

2 → 0) also left all 54 buckets credited (`w1/M01ShaOnlyHole.md`).

## 2. The rule (O, `.ufo/evidence/round-17/measure.py`)

This is a verifying trace (S058): record the hashes of what a step used, and
treat the result as current only while every recorded hash still matches. A
cache hit is sound only for what its key records (S059, S064).

- Every credited entry carries non-empty `inputs` (lane path → sha256). Each
  path must be a regular blob (mode 100644/100755) with that sha at the
  measured rev; otherwise `input-drift:`, `input-missing:` or `input-not-blob:`.
- An entry that executed commands names committed trace receipts whose
  inputs it covers (`traces-unrecorded`, `trace-missing:`,
  `trace-input-unrecorded:`). This holds for `record` and `instruction`
  entries alike, so relabelling a bucket does not escape it.
- A failing entry whose inputs still verify vetoes the bucket.
- `SKILL.md` itself and the ledger are not inputs: the bucket is already
  keyed by its own section sha, and the ledger is the output.

Red-before on real bytes, round-16 ledger plus the replayed round-14 inputs
(`.ufo/evidence/round-17/redbefore/legacy-r14-inputs.json`, 19 inputs traced
at `e69b488`): the bucket is `credited` at `e69b488` and
`input-drift:tools/mutate-and-run.sh` at `09ee1d0` and at `98bea7d`
(`redbefore/measure-*.json`). Those runs use `--inputs-overlay`, so they are
demonstrations; a cited score uses no override.

## 3. How inputs are recorded (O)

`.ufo/evidence/round-17/coldread/trace-inputs.py` runs a command under
`strace -f -y` (S060) in a clone of the lane at a 40-hex commit, and keeps
regular files opened read-only by name that are tracked at that commit.
Write-opened paths, untracked files and `.git/` are excluded; Python runs
with bytecode caching off, so a `.py` source is opened rather than a cached
`.pyc`. Fleet files outside the lane are listed as external, never credited.
A read of the live lane from a clone is flagged `live_lane_reads`.

## 4. Limits (O/I)

An open trace records files opened by name. It does not see environment
variables, stat-only checks, reads on inherited descriptors, directory
listings, network, the clock, or objects read through `git show REV:path`
(observed: `w1/S12StraceFeasibility.md`). Host binaries are outside the key,
the same false-hit class S059 documents for compilers outside a Bazel
workspace. A seat can still skip a command; the rule makes a recorded read
checkable, not complete.

### 3. R17-CMD-BIND: the narrower claim

The input-keyed rule binds credit to the recorded **inputs**. It does not bind
trace **argv** to the bucket's declared or required commands.

- Bound: each trace receipt's `inputs` must be covered by the entry's recorded
  `inputs` with a matching sha256 (`trace-input-unrecorded:`,
  `trace-input-drift:`; `measure.py:403-412`). An entry with
  `commands_executed_count > 0` needs at least one committed receipt in strict
  mode (`measure.py:368-380`).
- Not bound: `measure.py` never reads a receipt's `argv`. The only receipt-argv
  reference is the selftest fixture at `measure.py:773`. It also never reads
  `coldread/bucket-commands.json` (zero references at 183f87b). For example,
  `coldread/traces/CR01/1.json` records a `git -C … show <rev>:SKILL.md |
  sha256sum` argv, and nothing compares that argv with the bucket's declared
  commands.

So the rule shows that a recorded read ran against the recorded bytes. It is

# MTE report interop — tameshi ledger legs as mutation-testing-elements reports

## What the interop does

`tools/mte-interop.py --check` replays the eight recorded mutation-ledger legs
via `tools/mutate-and-run.sh --regression` (at the committed revision, or an
existing kept workdir via `--workdir`), emits one mutation-testing-elements
report per leg, validates it against the vendored official schema 3.9.0
(draft-07, python `jsonschema`), computes the official metrics with the
vendored `mutation-testing-metrics` 3.9.0 library (node `calculateMetrics`),
and judges four checks per leg: `schema`, `ledger`, `per_mutant`, `score`.
`ledger` compares the official killed, survived, invalid and total counts with
the runner's own REGRESSION_TABLE line; `per_mutant` compares every emitted
status with the committed recorded verdict of the same defect id in the
runner's TABLE_* lines. Those two are the checks that can fail on real data;
`score` is a sanity check that holds by construction. The leg set must be
exactly the eight ledger legs, or the run is SETUP (exit 2).

### Mapping: tameshi verdict → MTE report fields

| tameshi verdict | MTE `status` | `statusReason` |
|---|---|---|
| KILLED | Killed | tameshi verdict KILLED |
| SURVIVED | Survived | tameshi verdict SURVIVED |
| INCONCLUSIVE | RuntimeError | tameshi verdict INCONCLUSIVE |

(`tools/mte-interop.py:69`, `:152-157`.) The report is emitted per leg as:

- `schemaVersion: "1"` (matches the schema pattern `^([1-2])(\.(([1-9]\d*)|0)){0,2}$`);
- `thresholds: {high: 80, low: 60}` — required by the schema; both are integers
  0..100 (`:159`);
- `framework: {name: "tameshi mutate-and-run.sh"}` (`:160`);
- `files: {<target-basename>: {language, source, mutants}}` where
  - `source` = the pristine pinned target bytes, materialized from the repo's
    git object store by the runner;
  - `language` = from the target suffix: `.mjs`/`.js` → `javascript`,
    `.sh` → `shell`, `.py` → `python`, else `plaintext` (`:70`, `:158`);
    the eight legs are 4 shell + 4 javascript;
  - one mutant per recorded defect: `id` = defect id, `mutatorName` =
    `tameshi-hand-seeded`, `description` = defect description, `replacement` =
    the `@new` string, `location` derived from the defect's unique `@old`
    string, `status`/`statusReason` per the table above (`:152-157`);
  - `location.start` = 1-based line/column of the first byte of `@old`;
    `location.end` = 1-based line/column just past it (end-exclusive, matching
    the schema's "Start is inclusive, end is exclusive"). The `@old` string
    must occur exactly once in the pristine target; otherwise the leg is
    refused as SETUP, not judged (`:149-150`, `:126-129`).

## What the official schema and metrics library check

### Schema (S086; vendored 3.9.0, member `package/src/mutation-testing-report-schema.json`)

Root requires `schemaVersion`, `thresholds`, `files`; `thresholds` requires
`high` and `low` (integers 0..100); each file entry requires `language`,
`source`, `mutants`; each mutant requires `id`, `mutatorName`, `location`,
`status`; `status` must be one of the eight-value enum
(Killed/Survived/NoCoverage/CompileError/RuntimeError/Timeout/Ignored/Pending);
`location` requires `start` and `end`, each a position whose `line` and
`column` are integers ≥ 1; the `mutants` array has `uniqueItems: true`. The
tool validates with `jsonschema.Draft7Validator` (no FormatChecker), so the
single `format: uri` in `framework.homepageUrl` is not enforced; the schema
does not check locations against `source` or the truth of `statusReason`.
`S002` is the same schema file on GitHub master (byte-identical to the
vendored src member: sha256 404575e926…); `S086` pins the released 3.9.0 npm
package, which is what the tool validates against.

### Metrics (S087; vendored 3.9.0, `mutation-testing-metrics`)

`calculateMetrics(report.files)` counts mutants by status and computes
(`package/src/model/metrics.ts:39-42,50-58,69-73`; `package/src/calculateMetrics.ts:234-255`):

- `totalDetected = timeout + killed`;
- `totalUndetected = survived + noCoverage`;
- `totalValid = totalUndetected + totalDetected`;
- `totalInvalid = runtimeErrors + compileErrors`;
- `mutationScore = totalValid > 0 ? totalDetected / totalValid * 100 : NaN`;
- `mutationScoreBasedOnCoveredCode = totalDetected / totalCovered * 100`
  (`totalCovered = totalDetected + survived`), `0` when no coverage;
- `totalMutants = totalValid + totalInvalid + ignored + pending`.

The tool reads `mutationScore`, `killed`, `survived`, `totalValid`,
`totalInvalid`, `totalMutants` (`:81-85`, `:85`). The library only scores; it
does not validate the report against the schema (that is the separate
`jsonschema` step).

## INCONCLUSIVE and Timeout semantics

Tameshi's INCONCLUSIVE is "no definitive verdict": runner exit 124 (timeout),
126 (suite not executable), or 127 (suite not found)
(`tools/mutate-and-run.sh:539-541`); per `SKILL.md:208-212` it is not a kill
and is excluded from the kill-rate denominator (`killed/(killed+survived)`).
Mapping it to MTE `RuntimeError` makes the official library count it as
`totalInvalid` and exclude it from `totalValid` and the score. With no Timeout
and no NoCoverage mutants, the official score then equals
`killed/(killed+survived)*100` — tameshi's rate — by construction. Mapping the
exit-124 sub-case to MTE `Timeout` instead would count it as *detected*
(`totalDetected = timeout + killed`; S001: Timeout "is counted as 'detected'"),
making the official score `(k+t)/(k+s+t)`, which diverges from tameshi's rule
whenever `t > 0` and `s > 0`. The INCONCLUSIVE→RuntimeError mapping is
therefore a convention that preserves tameshi's arithmetic, not an equivalence
to Stryker semantics: the bucket also includes 126/127, and the report cannot
distinguish the sub-cases (`results.tsv` columns 1–2 only).

## Integer-percent rounding of the ledger

The runner's headline kill-rate is an integer percent:
`pct=$(( (200 * killed + total) / (2 * total) ))` at
`tools/mutate-and-run.sh:562`, where `total` is the number of spec defects
(`:499`) — round-half-up of `100·killed/total`. The interop judge and
`SKILL.md:210` use `killed/(killed+survived)`; these coincide only when
`inconclusive = 0` (true for all eight ledger legs). The recorded ledger
percentages are integers, e.g. `bash-checklist-run` 7/15 = 46.67 % is recorded
as 47 % (runner header `:90`; `SKILL.md:1103,1316`). The official score is a
float — for `bash-checklist-run` it is `46.666666666666664` (observed) — so
"official score equals the ledger's recorded percentage" is false for such a
leg; equality holds only against the unrounded fraction. The tool prints
`runner_pct` and `official_rounded_half_up` side by side as information; at
09dc114 the half-up rounding is `(200*k + k + s) // (2*(k+s))`, i.e.
round-half-up of `100·k/(k+s)` (`:321-334`).

## Reuse boundary

- The reports are validated against the *released* 3.9.0 schema and scored by
  the *released* 3.9.0 metrics library (sha512-pinned in `tools/vendor/`);
  a new release or an offset pin requires re-verification.
- The score equality is by construction under the 1:1 mapping; it is a sanity
  check, not an independent measurement (round-25 wave seat C2Tautology).
- The interop proves nothing about how Stryker would mutate these targets or
  score the same code; it is a format/score-semantics interop of tameshi's
  own ledger records.
- `INCONCLUSIVE→RuntimeError` is a tameshi convention, not a Stryker status
  equivalence; Timeout-as-detected is explicitly not adopted.
- No NoCoverage claim: the reports carry no `coveredBy`/`killedBy`, so
  `mutationScoreBasedOnCoveredCode` is not claimed; NoCoverage classification of
  the 35 recorded survivors stays open as frontier F1b. No producer
  authentication or promotion is claimed.
- The official web component (`mutation-testing-elements` 3.9.0) rendered all
  eight emitted reports headless with no errors and computed the same scores
  (round-25 seat C2HtmlRender). It is schema-lenient: a bogus status loads and
  is silently dropped from the tally. So the HTML consumer cannot replace the
  schema check; it only shows the reports are usable by the official viewer.

## Decision table — exporting a tameshi sweep as a report

| tameshi verdict | MTE status | in `valid`? | counts as detected? | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KILLED | Killed | yes | yes | S001 Killed; S087 `totalDetected = timeout + killed` |
| SURVIVED | Survived | yes | no | S001 Survived; never NoCoverage without coverage data |
| INCONCLUSIVE (exit 124/126/127) | RuntimeError | no | no | keeps tameshi's `k/(k+s)`; Timeout would count as detected (S001) |

Error patterns the selftest pins (`tools/mte-interop.py --selftest`):
`tameshi-vocabulary-status` (KILLED is not a schema status), `line-zero-location`
(positions start at one, S086), `timeout-is-not-a-tameshi-kill`,
`balanced-flip-same-counts` (counts agree but ids are swapped: only the
per-defect check against the recorded table sees it), `survived-as-nocoverage`.

## 4. What this case teaches

- **A mutation score is a property of a triple — gate, suite, harness.** The
  runner hands the suite a mutable environment (`MUTANT`, `WORKDIR`,
  `DEFECT_ID`, `tools/mutate-and-run.sh:452-456`) and lets the suite string
  build the sandbox. Any harness that puts the defect id into a path the suite
  prints can satisfy an unanchored assertion inside the suite. The check costs
  one extra sweep: re-run the ten defects with the sandbox renamed and compare.
  Any kill-aimed mutant that flips is a harness artifact, not a hole and not a
  kill.
- **Assert on the verdict line, not on a word.** `grep -q "$3"` over combined
  stdout+stderr that contains paths is satisfiable by an environment. Anchored
  forms (`grep -qE '^GONE '`, `grep -qE '^DRIFT_PINS: DRIFT'`) are not. This
  travels to kagi as a report line (adjacency), never as an edit here: tameshi
  reads the pinned bytes and recommends, it does not touch the gate.
- **A prediction table needs the mechanism, not only the verdict.** Three
  `KILLED` predictions missed for one reason that no prediction row names. The
  spec's per-row comments carry the reasoning; the composition line should
  carry the harness assumption too ("suite assertions must be
  environment-independent").

- Drift-chain presence: D5 dies on the single no-chain case — thin, but a working tripwire

- The fail-closed exit map: D8 dies on exactly the three fail-closed cases.
- Mode-floor value and checked accounting: D6 dies on the two loose-mode cases; the FIFO

  fixtures use partial-overlap modes (0o500 vs 0o700 floor; 0o400 vs 0o600 floor) that
  discriminate "contains the floor" from "intersects the floor". I: a suite that tested
  only modes sharing **no** floor bits (e.g. 0o000) would have missed this class.

  dangling symlink) — the secrecy cases double as leaf-pin guards.

**Not protected (measured gaps):**

- The verdict-line truncation boundary and its `+N more` arithmetic (D2): max findings in

- (I) Both gaps sit in the same region: reporting surfaces whose values no case reads.
  A caller consuming `--json` or the FAMILY lines is protected by nothing here.

**Scope (I):** this experiment mutates one artifact with single-text-edit defects. It does
not measure the live verify path against substrate drift (the suite's complement), and it

  a third gate: the asserted stem (exit + verdict word + `(` + per-case evidence substrings) is
  protected — all six kills are read through it — and a mutant confined to the verdict line's
  unasserted remainder survives (B9, §2). New shape: this gate's *only* full-roll-line assert

  all-HEALTHY one where every field reads the same; JS pinned its CLEAN line on the same

  now three points: JS one exact line + prefixes; kagi substring-only; tsukuroi prefix + an

  substrings, and B3 shows a fail-closed arm (empty-ring re-check) dying on exactly its 1 case.

## 5. Calibration and errata (append-only)

- **E1 — pre-registration held 10/10 on verdicts and 10/10 on failing-case counts** (B6's 21
  included), the first perfect sweep of the three. (I) Cause, recorded because it is not
  repeatable luck: both prior notes' E1 misses were *case-set* reasoning slips — this time the
  26 labels and their assert texts were parsed into tables (as §3.1 does) before the defects
  were written, so each predicted failing set came from the case grammar, not from memory. The
  advantage came from the two prior E1s; record it as method, not as skill.
- **E2 — incident errata (I1): the pin moved mid-run.** The assigned before/after sha claim is
  unsatisfiable (other writer). The record keeps both pins, the frozen copy's sha, and the
  write-fencing evidence. Method note (I): mutation cases on *concurrently edited* substrates
  need the pin to be a *committed revision* and the case to say so (it was, and does); the
  fleet's `mutate-and-run.sh` records the target sha before/after but cannot distinguish "the
  operator's run moved it" from "another lane moved it" — a mtime/inode note in its receipt
  would separate the two. Recommendation only; no tool edit from this lane (assignment bound).
- **E3 — band convention amendment (composition binding).** The kill-rate bands compare rates
  across sweeps; this case's 60 % is depressed by design (4 of 10 mutants were aimed at
  predicted holes). A rate without its composition (kill-aimed vs hole-aimed) is not comparable
  across authors — record composition beside every rate from now on. This does not move the
  bands; it binds them.
- **E4 — convergence, recorded as corroboration not as double-counting.** This sweep's survivor
  and hole classes (B7/B8/B9/B10, §3.2) overlap 8/9 with the concurrent lane's hardening classes
  (D02…D20). Two sweeps, two authors of the target, same holes — the strongest single datum in
  this note for rows D/E; it is *not* a second measurement of any cell in §1.

# Mutation-score semantics across tools

## Verdict vocabulary map

This maps outcome names, not interchangeable policies. Tameshi's rule is red **and** the full case count for Killed, green with the same count for Survived, and no definitive verdict for Inconclusive; only Killed and Survived enter its rate (`SKILL.md:191-213`).

| Tameshi | Stryker | cargo-mutants | mutmut (opened changelog only) | shmutant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Killed** — red + full count (`SKILL.md:191-194`) | **Killed** — at least one test fails (`S001 §Mutant states`, S001.html:11-12) | **caught** — a test fails (`S004 §Mutant outcomes`, S004.html:192-194) | No general verdict mapping in this changelog; it records only a timeout misclassification fix (`S005 HISTORY.rst:23`). | **killed** only if the named witness fails; red elsewhere is **accidental**, not a kill (`S006 §The three verdicts`, README:21-39). Tameshi records failing labels but no per-mutant witness, so its Killed cannot be split into these two (`SKILL.md:195-197`; S006 README:23-31). |
| **Survived** — green + full count (`SKILL.md:205-206`) | **Survived** or **NoCoverage** are both undetected; Stryker distinguishes them by test coverage (`S001 §Mutant states`, S001.html:13-16; §Metrics, :41-46). | **missed** — no test failed; docs say this may be a gap or an indistinguishable mutant (`S004 §Mutant outcomes`, S004.html:197-200). | No general mapping documented by the opened history (`S005 HISTORY.rst:1-46`). | **survived** means green (`S006 §The three verdicts`, README:27-31). |
| **Inconclusive** — timeout, crash before summary, or missing count is not a kill and is excluded (`SKILL.md:208-212`) | **Timeout** is counted as detected; runtime/compile errors are not in the score (`S001 §Mutant states`, S001.html:17-31; §Metrics, :39-52). Stryker's report schema enumerates eight statuses—`Killed`, `Survived`, `NoCoverage`, `CompileError`, `RuntimeError`, `Timeout`, `Ignored`, `Pending`—and requires each mutant's `id`, `mutatorName`, `location`, and `status` (`S002 mutation-testing-report-schema.json:41-46,88-100`). The exact source quotes, fetched URLs, access timestamps and SHA-256 values for all five reopened sources are retained in `.ufo/evidence/kaika-round-1/score-semantics/opened.tsv`; fetched bodies are retained there as `S001.html`, `S002.json`, `S004.html`, `S005.rst`, `S006.md`.

## Formula comparison

For the same valid mutant set, let `k` = killed, `s` = survived (including any NoCoverage mutants for the all-valid total), and `t` = timeouts. Tameshi uses `k/(k+s)` and excludes inconclusives (`SKILL.md:208-212`). Stryker defines detected as `k+t`, undetected as `s` (Survived + NoCoverage), valid as detected + undetected, and score as `detected/valid`; its compile/runtime errors are invalid and excluded (`S001 §Metrics`, S001.html:39-52; §Mutant states, :23-31). Thus, when the comparison contains only these valid outcomes, Stryker total score is `(k+t)/(k+s+t)`. Do not silently compare denominators if compile/runtime errors, ignored/pending mutants, or other unclassified cases are present: Stryker excludes them but Tameshi's formula does not define a corresponding bucket (`S001 §Metrics`, :45-52; `SKILL.md:208-212`).

For `k+s>0`:

`(k+t)/(k+s+t) - k/(k+s) = (t*s)/((k+s+t)(k+s)) >= 0`.

This is an inference from the cited formulas. The two total scores are equal exactly when `t=0` **or** `s=0` (with defined denominators); the `s=0` case matters even if timeouts occur. Stryker's separate covered-code score uses `covered = detected + survived`, so with `n` NoCoverage mutants among `s`, it is `(k+t)/(k+t+s-n)` (`S001 §Metrics`, S001.html:41-54). It is at least the overall score; a numeric covered-code score cannot be inferred without coverage-traced `n`.

## Rejected rule: “count Timeout as a kill”

Rejected for Tameshi's recorded score: a kill requires red **and** an enumerated full count (`SKILL.md:191-193`), while a timeout or run without a definitive summary is Inconclusive, not a kill (`SKILL.md:208-209`). A timed-out run therefore supplies no Tameshi kill/survivor denominator evidence; do not turn it into `k` or `s`. Stryker's Timeout-as-Detected policy is real but different (`S001 §Mutant states`, S001.html:17-22; §Metrics, :39-52). Flip only if the local scoring contract explicitly adopts that timeout-as-detected policy and records timeouts as a declared valid denominator category; merely observing a timeout is insufficient.

## 4. The opt-in protocol — running/commissioning a sweep

Sources: `corpus/knowledge/service-optin-protocol.md` (round 7, the two
measured engagements distilled) and the method-side rendering
`SKILL.md:794-897`.

**The offer.** Any lane may ask for a sweep of one of its gates. The queue is
an offer, not a schedule; a round with no opt-in records the no-opt-in line
as its complete outcome (`service-optin-protocol.md:26-30`;
`fleet-suite-census.md:269-291`). [U] how an opt-in reaches the service with

(`service-optin-protocol.md:264-266`).

**Request shape — what the opting-in lane brings** (`:54-77`,
`SKILL.md:806-825`):

1. a **pinned revision** — sha256, size, line count, mtime, porcelain-clean
   tree at open; a moved substrate needs a **re-pin, never a
   re-interpretation of the old table** (`:59-62`);
2. a **one-command hermetic suite** invocable on a copy — must exercise the
   copy it is handed, print its own executed count + verdict, read no live path;
3. a **clause-mapped defect spec** — one single-edit defect per declared
   clause, expectation pre-registered `killed|survived`;
4. nothing else.

Fill-in template (`:97-107`):

```
mode:       service | self-service | attestation
target:     <path> @ sha256 <…>, <B> B, <n> lines, mtime <…>; tree porcelain-clean at open
suite:      <one command with "$MUTANT">; prints own count + verdict; hermetic (no live path)
spec:       <n> single-edit defects, one per clause <A…>; @old uniqueness asserted; expect: pre-registered
evidence:   <corpus note path>   (the only fleet file the run writes)
scratch:    /tmp/w<N>-<lane>-*   (lane-scoped; foreign scratch never removed)
absorption: owner lane hardens + accepts; the service side is recommendations-only
```

**Read-only guarantees** (`:109-135`): the target is never a write target
(pristine copy; `MUTATE_RESTORE: OK` sha256 before = after); the sibling tree
stays clean before/after — the provable negative is "this lane's writes never
touched the gate"; the harness is pinned per run; no live substrate read
(PATH-level stubs only, never a session); all writes confined to scratch + the
one corpus note.

## 6. The cadence — the tick, the reading map, the triggers

The cadence is **a pin read executed at the tick** — three readings per case,
three triggers, one re-pin rule. No daemon, no timer: "standing" is the ledger
+ the policy + an executed command at the round boundary
(`SKILL.md:1010-1019`; executed first at round 9, `:1155-1163`). [U] whether

**The reading map** (`SKILL.md:1031-1036`):

| reading | rule | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `current` | `git show <tip>:<path>` sha == recorded pin (`<tip>` = branch tip, not HEAD) | swept bytes are the gate's live blob |
| `stale` | recorded revision is an ancestor of `<tip>`, live blob differs | gate moved past the recorded revision; the table is historical, not wrong |
| `drift` | worktree differs from the branch tip (porcelain non-empty, or live sha ≠ tip blob sha) | uncommitted bytes; a hygiene reading — git-materialized replays are already immune |
| tool `held` / `moved` | harness sha == / ≠ the sha on the last `REGRESSION_TOOL`/`MUTATE_TOOL` line | the instrument moved since the table was measured |

**Triggers — what to do** (`SKILL.md:1069-1090`):

- **T1 — a case reads `stale`** → re-measure at the live revision, or record
  the STALE cell with its reason; never edit the recorded table.
- **T2 — the harness sha ≠ the revision a case was measured under** → re-run
  the reproduction under the new revision and record both pins (precedent:
  mado's spec re-cut under `b56c6e57…`, identical verdicts and mutant shas).
- **T3 — an owner records a re-run at a new revision** → an appended row;
  §1–§4 never edited.
- **The re-pin rule:** a moved pin is never re-interpreted against the new
  bytes; both revisions stay in the record; `moved=0 stale=0` is a complete
  outcome, recorded as such (drift is never manufactured by re-cutting
  cases). A `drift` reading waits for the owner's jj-lane commit (cite the pushed hash), then re-pins
  (`SKILL.md:1083-1086`; `fleet-kill-rate-ledger.md:293`, `:310`;
  `service-optin-protocol.md:59-62`).

**The tick is a timestamped observation, re-run at the next boundary — never
carried as a standing claim** (`SKILL.md:1188-1189`).

## 8. The operator's full loop — commissioning to append

1. **Tick** (§0, §6) at the round boundary: tool pin → `--selftest` →
   `--regression` → six-case pin read → classify readings → T1–T3.
2. **On `stale`:** no action on the recorded table; either re-measure the live
   revision (a new sweep at the new pin) or append a STALE cell with its
   reason; both revisions stay in the record (T1, §6).
3. **On `drift`:** wait for the owner's jj-lane commit (cite the pushed hash), then re-pin; nothing is re-interpreted
   against a moving file (§6, `service-limits.md` row c).
4. **On tool `moved`:** re-run the reproduction under the new revision and
   record both pins (T2).
5. **On FAIL:** quote the `REGRESSION_DEFECT`/`TABLE` rows; never hand-re-sweep
   to confirm; the divergence is the finding (§7).
6. **On SETUP:** fix the environment (repo/rev/pin), never re-interpret the
   recorded table (§7).
7. **New opt-in:** take the request shape (§4) → run per §2 → the corpus note
   is the only fleet file the run writes → owner absorbs with its own ledger →
   the outcome lands as an **appended row or errata block** in
   `fleet-kill-rate-ledger.md` (§3; ER-3 `:312`).
8. **A submission to become a leg** needs the contribution contract: pinned
   file set (path + revision + sha256), a defect spec (`@old` unique,
   `@new != @old`), a one-command hermetic suite with `$MUTANT`, and the
   recorded verdict table as its expectation (`SKILL.md:954-963`). [U] no
   fleet-contributed leg exists yet.
9. **Nothing else is promised:** no daemon, no timer, no schedule — "who runs
   it" is the operator's standing choice; the service's refusals stand (§5).

# Oracle-anchored survivor classification — cite-check holes (round 27)

## 1. The question

Round 26 called four of the five `cite-check.mjs` survivors suite holes
(`mutation-case-kumitate-cite-check.md` §4). Each call rests on an off-suite
witness that runs the pristine and the mutant and finds a difference. The
pristine output is the expected value. S012 names that kind of expectation
**state-anchored**: it "flows, directly or transitively, from" the code under
mutation, so if the pristine were itself wrong on the witness input, the
differential would still report a hole, and it would also report a hole when
the mutant is the correct one. A **specification-anchored** expectation is
"composed from values fixed outside the code under mutation" (S012 abstract).

This entry re-judges the four holes with specification-anchored expectations
and records which anchor holds each one.

## 2. Method (executed)

1. For each survivor, write the expected exit status and finding kind from
   anchors outside the mutated statement, before any run
   (`.ufo/evidence/round-27/f8/anchors.json`, committed in `06a6707`):
   - **contract**: a header comment line of the pinned blob. The test this
     entry applies (tighter than "outside the mutated statement", after wave
     seat CriticAnchors): no code line and no run of the mutated file supplies
     the value. A header comment is not executed and all four mutated
     statements are code lines.
   - **external**: a SOURCES row opened this round.
   - **arithmetic**: a fact the probe computes from the witness bytes it
     wrote (here, the newline count of the cited file).
2. Run the pristine and the mutant on the survivor's witness tree under
   `env -i` (`.ufo/evidence/round-27/f8/anchor-probe.py`). Compare each run
   with the anchored expectation, not with the other run.
3. Class: `anchored-hole` when the pristine meets the anchor and the mutant
   does not; `anchor-disagrees-with-pristine` when the pristine misses it (a

# A property-based generator for a fixture gate: written to the gate's contract, observed by class, scored by mutants it never saw

Round 49 (claim C2) built one generator, `tools/pbt-staged-id.py`, against one named gate, `tools/staged-id-guard.py`
(the round-43 pre-adoption id guard, sha256 `03a796c5…`, never edited). This entry states what the two sources teach
about generators, what the lane built from it, how the build is measured, and what the measurement does not reach.
Measured values live in the deciding receipt `.ufo/evidence/round-49/after/c2.stdout`, never in this text.

## What the sources state

- **A property is an executable function over random input, and the generator is a separate artefact the tester writes.**
  S269, Abstract (p. 268): "Properties are described as Haskell functions, and can be automatically tested on random
  input". §2.4 (p. 270): "QuickCheck provides support for the programmer to define his or her own test data generators,
  with control over the distribution of test data".
- **The distribution must be observed, not assumed.** S269, §2.4 (p. 270): "The combinator collect will gather all values
  that are passed to it, and print out a histogram of these values." §5.1.4 (p. 274) names the failure this guards
  against: "the false sense of security that can be engendered when one's program passes a large number of tests in
  trivial cases".
- **Size is the tester's knob.** S269, §3.2 (p. 271): `sized` "generates an a by passing the current size bound to its
  parameter", and "It is then up to the programmer to interpret the size bound in some reasonable way during test data
  generation."
- **The generator must fit the program at hand.** S270, §2.10 (printed p. 34): "the quality of the test data determines
  the quality of the generated equations", and "it is important to provide good test data generators, that fit the
  program at hand"; the same page warns that "creating custom generators is sometimes necessary to get correct results".

## What the lane built

- **Run through the CLI only; the oracle re-implements the guard's rules.** At run time the generator never imports,
  execs or opens the guard (an access trace shows it opens only the `--guard` path it is handed, as a subprocess;
  `.ufo/waves/round-49/w2/T49W2ExecGenTrace.md`); it runs `python3 -I GUARD --registry R --staged G [--map M] --json`
  per case and checks the answer against its own oracle: the CORPUS census row rule (0-3 leading spaces), collisions
  sorted by number, held/unmapped by form-insensitive document key, the naive map and its cascade, and the
  map-validation rules. The oracle is not independent in derivation: a wave-2 critic found its regexes byte-identical
  to the guard's and its analysis largely transcribed from the guard's source, undocumented thresholds included
  (`.ufo/waves/round-49/w2/T49W2CritGenOracle.md`). It therefore catches a guard that departs from its own round-43
  rules, not a rule the round-43 author got wrong.
  The guard's exit semantics are taken as observed (0 answered/admitted, 1 analysis refused or map inadmissible,
  2 setup refusal); its module docstring names exit 1 only for an inadmissible map — a documentation imprecision recorded
  in `corpus/lessons/round-49.md`, not a guard edit.
- **Fit to the program at hand (S270).** Cases are small markdown registries and staged tables (two to eight rows across the
  pair) built from per-class recipes: indentation 0-6 spaces including 4+ (not a row under the census), ids of 3-6 digits, duplicate ids
  and short rows (must refuse), URL form variants (scheme, `www.`, case, trailing slash), undocumented rows, cascades,
  and admissible and inadmissible maps for each map rule.
- **Distribution printed, per class (S269 §2.4).** Every run prints the count of each of twelve classes (the frozen
  list in `.ufo/evidence/round-49/contract.json` `claims.C2.classes`); the round-49 counter recomputes the classes from
  the dump with its own predicates and requires at least 10 cases each at seed 4949, 400 cases.
- **Deterministic and replayable.** `random.Random(seed)`; the dump holds every case run; the first violation stops the
  run and names its index (the counterexample).

## How it is measured, and the control

The frozen counter `.ufo/evidence/round-49/c2/measure.py` runs the generator on the pristine guard (no violation
allowed, and its own oracle must agree with the guard on every analysis case), then on each mutant of a twelve-mutant
panel that was hidden from the generator's author until the deciding run (commit-reveal: the contract pins its sha256).
A mutant counts only when the generator's counterexample makes the pristine and the mutant guard print different
answers (differential confirmation). The fixture-replay control — the guard's own 14 selftest fixtures with golden
outputs, through the same interface — confirms 6 of the 12 (`.ufo/evidence/round-49/control/c2-controls.stdout`); a
hand-made witness set confirms all 12, so no panel mutant is equivalent.

## What this does not establish

- One generator against one lane-owned gate: F10's "one generator against a named fixture gate" move, not a method
  shown across the fleet's gates.
- No shrinking: a counterexample is the first failing case, not a minimal one.
- The counter cannot tell a property-based generator from a differential one that compares the mutant with a copy of
  the pristine guard (wave-1 critic, `.ufo/waves/round-49/w1/T49CritC2Contract.md` F1); the evidence that this one is
  property-based is outside the counter: its code (CLI calls only, its own oracle), an access trace and oracle-mutation
  results in the round-49 wave-2 reports.
- Twelve mutants are a small panel; a kill count is a measurement of this panel, not a mutation score of the guard.
- Guard behaviours the distribution cannot reach (wave-2 mutation seats, blind to the panel): a 5-cell row (the
  short-row boundary), duplicate keys in a map's JSON, the two input sha256 fields, oversized or non-regular inputs
  (`.ufo/waves/round-49/w2/T49W2MutGuardOwn.md`, `T49W2ExecC2Probe.md`). Three oracle rules no generated case
  exercises (numeric collision order past the digit-width boundary, the 5-cell boundary, the 12-character id cap;
  `T49W2MutGenerator.md`). These are the next generator moves, not claimed here.

# PIT and Stryker name the same outcomes and score them differently

Assimilated from the shokuknow `corpus-expansion-1` package (`staged:S159`, `staged:S160`
renumbered to S155, S156), re-grounded in round 42 against pages this lane opened itself;
S158 is new this round. Gate: `corpus/lessons/round-42.md`.

## What the sources state

- PIT reports one of seven outcomes per mutation (S155, §"Running the tests", snapshot
  line 163: "For each mutation PIT will report one of the following outcomes"): Killed,
  Survived, No coverage, Non viable, Timed Out, Memory error, Run error.
- Two of those outcomes are easy to merge and PIT keeps them apart (S155, snapshot
  line 179): "No coverage is the same as Survived except there were no tests that
  exercised the line of code where the mutation was created" (23 words).
- A run error is not a kill in PIT's vocabulary (S155, snapshot lines 175, 192):
  "Killed means a test caught the mutation successfully." (8 words) and "A run error means
  something went wrong when trying to test the mutation." (13 words).
- PIT's results are not fully deterministic (S156, §"Is it random?", snapshot line 293):
  "Pitest works hard to be fully deterministic, but two factors might cause the results
  to differ slightly between two runs with the same input." (24 words). The FAQ names
  two factors, timeouts and static initializers; for the first it says "a mutant may be
  detected as timed out on one run, but killed or surviving on another" (§Timeouts,
  snapshot lines 298–299, 17 words).
- PIT's code scores a run error as detected (S158, snapshot line 63, `RUN_ERROR(true)`;
  the boolean is the `detected` field returned by `isDetected()`, lines 78 and 108).
  `getForErrorExitCode` (line 91) maps every non-zero child exit that is neither out of
  memory nor a timeout to `RUN_ERROR`.
- Stryker, which the lane already holds (S001, `corpus/SOURCES.md:12`), does the
  opposite. Its Runtime error state "is not represented in your mutation score"
  (S001 snapshot re-opened 2026-10-25, `.ufo/evidence/round-42/sources/stryker-mutant-states.html`
  line 26), and runtime errors count as invalid, outside `detected / valid`.

## What this means for the lane

- **Same label, different score.** Observation: PIT and Stryker both separate "run
  error" from "killed" by name (S155, S001). Observation: PIT counts it as detected
  (S158); Stryker leaves it out of the score (S001). Inference: two reports can quote
  the same mutation score while one of them counts crashes as detections. A score
  quoted without its outcome classes and their treatment cannot be compared across
  these two tools. That answers the lane's F1 interop question in the negative for
  this pair.
- **The lane's own rule sides with neither tool's treatment of timeouts.** The lane's
  rule makes a timeout or a crash before the summary Inconclusive, not a kill, and
  keeps it out of the rate (`SKILL.md:208-212`, mapped in
  `corpus/knowledge/mutation-score-semantics.md:10` and `:71`). Stryker counts a timeout as
  detected (S001); PIT's code does too (S158, `TIMED_OUT(true)`, line 37). Held S001
  semantics describe Stryker. They do not describe the lane's recorded convention.
  S156 adds a reason for the lane's choice: a timeout verdict depends on machine load.
- **What a lane report must publish.** Publish the outcome classes and say how each
  class enters the denominator, not just the percentage. The round-42 census counter
  follows this rule for its own mutants: a crash or unparseable output is
  `runtime_error`, never `killed` (`.ufo/evidence/round-42/census/measure.py`, oracle).
  That is the lane's rule and Stryker's, not PIT's.

## Boundary of this entry

- PIT's vocabulary is PIT's; this entry sets PIT's and Stryker's side by side and
  does not map one onto the other.
- S158 is a source file pinned at one upstream commit, not a documented contract;
  PIT can change `DetectionStatus` without a docs change. A later round must re-open
  it at the then-current head before relying on it.
- The PIT path `pitest.org/quickstart/mutationcoverage/` returned HTTP 404 on
  2026-10-25. The two docs pages above are the live carriers of the outcome
  definitions.
- No PIT run was executed. The scoring claim rests on PIT's source, not on a
  measured report.

# A literal-line census cannot see a destination held in a variable

## What the sources state

- S153 (CPython's own `ast` reference): "The ast module helps Python applications to
  process trees of the Python abstract syntax grammar." (15 words). The page documents
  the node types the resolver uses — `Name`, `Assign`, `Call`, `Attribute` — and
  `ast.get_source_segment`, which returns the source segment for a node and `None` when
  location information is missing. `iter_child_nodes` yields direct children only;
  `ast.walk` is the recursive walker. The parse keeps a call site and the assignment that
  feeds its argument in one tree, which is the property a line-oriented matcher lacks.
- S154 (`Path.write_text`): "Open the file pointed to in text mode, write data to it,
  and close the file:" (16 words). The signature is `Path.write_text(data, encoding=None,
  errors=None, newline=None)` — it has no destination parameter, so for `Path` the file
  written is the path the method is called on. `Path.write_bytes(data, …)` takes the same
  shape. This is why the receiver, not an argument, is the destination for that write
  form.

Neither source says anything about static analysis of a fixture census. They supply the
two mechanisms the tool uses: a tree that keeps assignment and call together, and the
receiver-as-destination rule for the path-method write form.

## The measured finding

At the round-41 freeze revision, `tools/write-path-census-v2.py` (round 40) reads one
line at a time and requires the expected-value token to be a literal on that line.
`tools/write-path-census-v3.py` resolves it instead. On `tools/repeat-control.py`:

| site | form | what v3's trace resolves | v2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `:811` | `with open(duplicate_path, "wb")` | the `expected.json` literal under `duplicate_path`, three hops from `scratch = tempfile.mkdtemp(…, dir="/tmp")` at `:597` | write site yes, expected-value destination no — the destination is the bare name `duplicate_path` |
| `:820` | `os.symlink(…, os.path.join(tamper_manifest_symlink, "expected.json"))` | the expected-value destination, rooted at the same `scratch` | no write site at all (`os.symlink` is outside its pattern), and the literal sits on the next line |

The record field is a concatenation of the source segments the resolver consulted, not a
normalized filesystem path: reading it as `…/snap-tamper-duplicate-key/expected.json`
overstates it. `expected=1 scratch=1 unflagged=0` is the honest reading of both rows.

Both live sites are scratch fixtures, so both are correctly exempt from the "unflagged
write path" count. The capability the round adds is **visibility of the destination**,
not a new open write path.

### Known false-positive class (disclosed, not fixed here)

A census over the whole `tools/` directory reports three `unflagged` sites. Two are false
positives: `tools/context-capture.py:1682` and `:1685`. Both are scratch in fact —
`expected_path = os.path.join(directory, "expected.json")` is rooted at
`directory = self.case_dir(name)`, and `self.root = tempfile.mkdtemp(…, dir="/tmp")`.
`_bind` records plain `Name` targets only, so `self.root` never enters the environment,
and a non-folding call still contributes its own source text; the destination therefore
resolves to a non-empty string with no scratch marker, and the tool scores it `unflagged`.
The third, `tools/registry-replay.py:123`, is a real non-scratch write of
`expected.json` into an explicit `--out` directory; the census counts it because an
explicit output flag is not in the update-flag pattern. That is a classification gap, not
a hidden update.

The rule for reading the tool's `unflagged` column is therefore: **verify the base
expression**. The fix (dotted-attribute binding plus a completeness flag, so a destination
whose base does not fold can never score `unflagged`) is routed to the next round; this
round's claim names two live sites and claims no directory-wide count.

`os.replace` / `os.rename` are recorded with both arguments as destinations, so a *read*
of an expected file can be listed beside its write. `tools/repeat-control.py` has no such
site; the seven in `tools/` all resolve `expected=False`, so no measured count changes.

## The method, bounded

Parse with `ast`; walk statements in source order; bind `Name -> value` for plain and
annotated assignment and `with … as`; resolve a destination through `os.path.join`, `+`,
`/`, `JoinedStr` and attribute chains to a depth of four; then classify the resolved text
as expected-value (`expected.json`, `expected.txt`, `.expected`, `golden`, `snapshot`) or
scratch (`/tmp`, `tempfile`, `TemporaryDirectory`, `NamedTemporaryFile`, `mkdtemp`,
`scratch`). A `Call` node contributes its own source text plus its arguments' resolved text, so
`pick("expected.json", …)` reads as expected whatever it returns: the record is a trace, not a path. The update flag (`--update_goldens`, `--update-goldens`, `--update`,
`update_goldens`) is read from the whole file, not from the call site. A scratch marker
seen anywhere in the resolution trace exempts the site, so a variable rooted in the
scratch directory is exempted rather than mistaken for a repo-level write — while a
variable rooted at a fixture directory that is not scratch stays counted.

## Prior art (adjacent; reported, not absorbed)

Two sibling tools already resolve write destinations through assignments:
`kotodama-shokunin/tools/harness/round_runner_conformance.py` (a five-pass constant
fixpoint to depth 8) and `kotodama-shokunin/tools/harness/receipt_guard_adoption.py`

# An attribute or an output flag can carry a write destination that a line-local census misreads

## What the sources state

- S157, §dest, snapshot lines 1504–1505: "For optional argument actions, the value of
  dest is normally inferred from the option strings." (15 words). Lines 1512–1514: "Any
  internal - characters will be converted to _ characters to make sure the string is a
  valid attribute name." (20 words). So `add_argument('--out-dir')` puts the value at
  `ns.out_dir`, and the destination of a write rooted at `ns.out_dir` is whatever the
  operator passed on the command line **when the option has no default** (S157 §default,
  snapshot lines 1209–1211: "The default keyword argument of add_argument() specifies what
  value should be used if the command-line argument is not present." — 18 words;
  `set_defaults()` supplies the same).
- S157, §The parse_args() method, lines 1650–1651: "Convert argument strings to objects
  and assign them as attributes of the namespace. Return the populated namespace."
  (17 words). That is the binding the tool checks for: the namespace must come from a
  `parse_args(...)` call before an attribute read counts as an option value.
- S153 (held since round 41) supplies the syntax tree the tool walks.

## The three live misreads (v3) and what v4 does

| site | v3 | why | v4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tools/context-capture.py:1682`, `:1685` | `unflagged=1` | the base is `self.case_dir(name)`; v3 cannot see that `case_dir` returns `os.path.join(self.root, …)` or that `self.root = tempfile.mkdtemp(…, dir="/tmp")` (`:1624`, `:1631-1635`) | `scratch=1`, `unflagged=0`; resolved text carries `mkdtemp` |
| `tools/registry-replay.py:123` | `unflagged=1` | `out` is a parameter of `publish`; both in-module calls pass `out = Path(args.out)` (`:181`, `:185`) or `Path(a.out)` (`:282`), and `--out` is declared at `:259` | `explicit_out=1`, `unflagged=0`; resolved text ends `argparse --out` |

v4 (`tools/write-path-census-v4.py`) adds three bounded steps to v3's walk:

1. **Attribute binding.** Every `self.<attr> = <expr>` in any method of the enclosing
   class is collected. An attribute with exactly one distinct plain assignment resolves to
   it. Two or more distinct expressions, or any augmented assignment, leave it unresolved,
   so it is never read as scratch — for the plain-assignment shapes the collector sees.
   Tuple targets, starred targets, `for self.x in …`, `with … as self.x`, walrus and
   `setattr(self, …)` are not collected, so a second binding through any of those shapes
   does not make the attribute ambiguous.
2. **Method-return fold.** `self.<m>(…)` for a same-class method with exactly one
   top-level `return <expr>` resolves to that expression, evaluated in the method's own
   top-level assignments. Nested returns are ignored, so a method whose reachable branch
   returns a golden path but also carries a top-level `return` of a scratch path is folded
   to the scratch path.
3. **Output-flag trace.** For `--out`, `--output`, `--out-dir` and `--output-dir`, the
   dest is derived as S157 states, or taken from `dest=`. A destination is `explicit_out`
   when its root resolves to `<ns>.<dest>` with `<ns>` bound to a `parse_args(...)` result.
   It is also `explicit_out` when its root is a parameter of a module-level function and
   every in-module call passes, at that position, an expression that does. A single
   call with any other argument (a constant, an `--input` value) keeps the site unflagged.
   `default=`, `const=` and `set_defaults()` values are **not** checked: an option with a
   default still labels the destination `explicit_out` although the write then lands in the
   default path without the operator naming it.

Resolution depth rises from four to eight hops: the context-capture chain needs six.
`--json` prints every write site with `explicit_out` beside v3's fields; text mode keeps
v3's per-site line format (without v3's totals line).

## The kill oracle used to test it

The round-42 counter (`.ufo/evidence/round-42/census/measure.py`) mutates v4 and runs a
ten-fixture battery plus the three live sites out of process. A mutant is `killed` only
when every run completes with parseable output and at least one case differs from its
declared classification. A crash, a Traceback or unparseable output is `runtime_error`,
and a run with no differing case is `survived`. This matches the lane's own verdict rule:
a crash before the summary is Inconclusive, not a kill (`SKILL.md:208-209`). It also
matches Stryker, whose Runtime error state "is not represented in your mutation score"
(S001, snapshot line 26, 8 words). PIT scores the same class as detected (S158,
`RUN_ERROR(true)`, line 63), so the oracle follows Stryker and the lane, not PIT.
`corpus/knowledge/pit-outcome-vocabulary.md` records that divergence. The counter's own
docstring cites PIT and Stryker together for this rule; that citation is half wrong and
is corrected in the round-42 contract's post-freeze amendments (the counter bytes are
pinned and are not edited).

## What is not claimed

- Not a dataflow analyser. The bounded steps above are not sound: the wave-2 attack seats
  found v4 clearing repo-landing expected-value writes as `scratch`/`explicit_out` in 23
  constructed shapes (CriticV4Wrong) and more in the reviewer's and critics' probes
  (ReviewV4Entry, ReviewV4Source, CriticSourced, MutProbeMethod). Known false-negative
  classes (each hides a real expected-value write):
  - parameter shadowing: a function parameter does not shadow a module-level binding, so
    `def emit(ns): … ns.out …` after a module-level `ns = ap.parse_args()` borrows the
    global namespace;
  - nested functions and loops: `_bind` does not bind `for` targets or nested-function
    parameters, so a loop or inner function that assigns a golden path inside a flagged
    function still reads as explicit;
  - starred-argument misalignment: `emit(*pair, ns.out)` shifts positions, so the wrong
    parameter is traced;
  - non-plain attribute rebinds: tuple/starred targets, `setattr(self, …)`, class-body
    assignments, subclass rebinding and template-method overrides evade the ambiguity rule
    and read as scratch;
  - `default=` / `set_defaults` on an output option (label `explicit_out` although the
    operator never named the destination);
  - calls through variables, `functools.partial`, `getattr`, dicts, sub-parsers sharing a
    dest, and `os.path.join` with an absolute later component;
  - the whole-resolved-text substring test: `/tmp` inside `tmpl` or an identifier such as
    `scratch_root` flips `scratch`;
  - two-destination writes (`os.replace` over two `--out` paths) never count as
    `explicit_out`.
- `flagged` stays file-global, as in v3: an update-flag string anywhere in the file
  marks every site flagged, and a short `--update` option flags the whole file.
- `explicit_out` says the operator *can* name the destination; because of the `default=`
  gap it does not prove the write lands where the operator chose.
- The counter's frozen battery cannot tell a resolver from a tool that special-cases the
  battery's names and line numbers. The wave-1 critic built one (a v3 copy with literal
  tables) that passes every fixture and live check. The round-42 records carry the
  renamed-identifier falsifier that separates the two (`corpus/lessons/round-42.md`).
- No new open write path is claimed in this lane's tools; with v4 the lane's tracked
  `tools/` Python files (26) census 0 unflagged sites, and that count is the only live
  claim the frozen counter makes.

(`.ufo/waves/round-42/w1/ConnectorSibling.md`). The round-41 prior art (kotodama's

# Anchor-refresh rule — when a registry row's snapshot digest drifts

## The rule

`CORPUS.md`'s SOURCES.md rule 2 makes the registry append-only: only `status`,
`recheck` and `used-by` change in place; a correction is a new row whose
`teaches` opens `supersedes S0NN —`. A stale `anchor` cell (a digest that no
longer matches the live document) is therefore repaired by a **new supersede
row**, never by editing the old row's anchor cell in place. The old row stays
as history; the new row pins the fresh snapshot and names what it supersedes.

## When it fires

- The live document changes bytes but the cited text survives at the same
  offsets (measured by sha256 change with identical located quotes). Example:
  S089 (2026-10-22 anchor digest `bc572676…`) vs the 2026-10-25 re-open
  (`79f6501a…`); the sentences at lines 15–16 are byte-identical.
- The document moves anchor (heading/paragraph/section), so the old `anchor`
  cell's location no longer resolves. The new row records the new location.

## The evidence discipline

- A new supersede row must be opened in the round that writes it: the round
  lesson's `## Gate` records the URL, the access date, and a ≤25-word located
  quote with its line.
- The change is logged old→new in that round's lesson.
- The census must stay exit 0; a duplicate-URL W04 warning (the same document
  held under the superseded row) is a warning, not an E-code.
- The new row is `mined` only when a knowledge entry or lesson cites it
  (`used-by` non-empty); the record-agreement class m7 then reads it as a
  real row.

## Why not edit in place

An in-place anchor edit rewrites history: a reader of the old row cannot tell
which digest was checked when, and a later audit cannot reconstruct the drift.
The supersede row keeps both facts visible (old digest in S089, new digest in
S160) and satisfies the record-agreement citation grammar: S160 is a registry
row; `key=S###` receipt fields are values, not citations.

# The rerun that decides a failure is flaky runs in the same job; these authors found the misses by rerunning in a fresh environment

## What the snapshot records

The record is the authors' institutional publication page (`portal.fis.tum.de`, a Pure portal), not the publisher's PDF. It carries the abstract, the DOI, the citation block, the bibliographic details and the portal's derived Fingerprint block, and nothing else about the paper's content beyond two abstract sentences this entry does not quote.

- Authors: Fabian Leinen, Martin Gruber, Saadet Sena Erdogan, Andreas Stahlbauer, Alexander Pretschner; affiliations Informatics 4 – Chair of Software and Systems Engineering (Technical University of Munich), BMW AG, CQSE GmbH (snapshot §header, visible text).
- Venue and identity: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering; DOI 10.1109/TSE.2026.3729363; state `Accepted/In press - 2026` (snapshot §details). The snapshot carries no publication day: `grep -c '2026-09-19' <snapshot>` → `0`.
- Keywords: continuous integration, empirical study, flaky tests, software testing, test reliability (snapshot §keywords).
- Access marker: the DOI list item carries `class="open-access"` in the markup around the DOI link (snapshot §Access to Document). The marker is markup; the page's visible text does not spell out a licence.

## Located quotes (verbatim, with their occurrence count)

The abstract is served four times on the page — the visible abstract, the BibTeX `abstract` field, the RIS `N2` field and the RIS `AB` field — so most sentences occur four times; the three that carry escaped characters occur three times, because the BibTeX block writes them as `{\textquoteright}`, `{\textendash}` and `{\texttimes}`. Token counts below are over the counter's own `fold()` of the quote; occurrence counts are `grep -oF '<quote>' | wc -l` over `python3 .ufo/evidence/round-45/freshness/measure.py --extract <snapshot>`.

1. "Flaky tests produce non-deterministic outcomes, passing or failing inconsistently when executed under conditions that developers intend to maintain constant" — 19 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
2. "Modern CI systems commonly rerun failed tests within the same job to identify flaky failures" — 15 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
3. "Existing research predominantly analyzes data from this detection mechanism, overlooking undetected flaky failures that cause the most severe disruptions" — 19 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
4. "All apparently deterministic failures were systematically validated through reruns in fresh environments within the projects' original CI infrastructure" — 18 tokens, 3 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
5. "We found that, across all projects, undetected flaky failures account for 9.8 %–16.3 % of failed pipeline runs" — 18 tokens, 3 occurrences; the package copy carries this sentence with its second clause in bold markers.
6. "These flaky failure rates spike temporarily, triggered primarily by code changes and test reordering" — 14 tokens, 4 occurrences, present in the package copy.
7. "While failures concentrate heavily in small test case subsets" — 9 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
8. "the most disruptive test cases with undetected flaky failures remain largely invisible to tools relying on current detection mechanisms" — 19 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
9. "Additionally, test environments significantly influence flakiness, with up to 3× variation in flake rates between them" — 16 tokens, 3 occurrences, absent from the package copy.
10. "Our publicly available dataset of 154,000 flaky test cases with 1.7 million flaky failures provides an empirical foundation" — 18 tokens, 4 occurrences, absent from the package copy (the sentence continues past the quoted span: "for developing improved strategies for industrial CI environments").

The dash form of quote 5 needs naming: the visible abstract and both RIS fields render `9.8 %–16.3 %` (en dash, spaces before the percent signs); the BibTeX block renders `9.8 \%{\textendash}16.3 \%`; and the lane's extractor folds the three visible copies to `9.8 %-16.3 %` while leaving the BibTeX copy escaped as `9.8 \%{\textendash}16.3 \%` (counts over the extraction: `3` and `1`), so a plain `grep -F '9.8 %–16.3 %'` over the extraction returns `0` while `grep -F '9.8 %-16.3 %'` returns `3`. The counter's `fold()` maps the en dash to the ASCII hyphen, so the visible spelling and the extractor's spelling both match a quoted span; the BibTeX `{\textendash}` spelling matches neither and is not quoted here.

## The mechanism, in the source's own terms

Observation, from quotes 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8: the abstract says modern CI systems commonly rerun failed tests **within the same job** to identify flaky failures (2); that apparently deterministic failures were validated through reruns **in fresh environments inside the projects' original CI infrastructure** (4); that undetected flaky failures are 9.8 %–16.3 % of failed pipeline runs (5); that failures concentrate heavily in small test case subsets (7); and that the most disruptive undetected cases remain largely invisible to tools relying on current detection mechanisms (8). Inference: the abstract does not say that the four studied projects' own detector was the same-job rerun; it says that mechanism is the common one.

Observation, from quote 1: the definition of the phenomenon is a test whose outcome varies "under conditions that developers intend to maintain constant" — the intent to hold conditions constant is part of the definition, not an assumption about them.

Observation, from quote 10: the paper ships a dataset of 154,000 flaky test cases and 1.7 million flaky failures.

## What this adds to F3

The ground F3 already has behind it (the frontier row stays `open`) is a repeated-control precondition with a finite sample: `corpus/README.md:127` records the scope of `knowledge/repeated-control-precondition.md` ("A standalone exact-tuple repeated-control gate; a clean result is finite sample agreement, not proof of determinism or a flaky-test cure"), and `corpus/README.md:80` states the next move as "N ≥ 3 byte-identical controls, or a named mismatch". The lane's F5 entry already refuses the stronger claim (`corpus/knowledge/hermetic-env-differential.md:4`: F3 universal determinism and successor freshness remain unclaimed).

The stated framing: "This study represents an inflection point by challenging the deep-seated assumption that flaky test failures are isolated occurrences" (18 tokens).

**The data.** "We used an established dataset of 10,000 test suite runs from 24 Java projects on GitHub, spanning domains from data orchestration to job scheduling" (24 tokens); "It contains 810 flaky tests, which we levered to perform a mixed-method empirical analysis of co-occurring flaky test failures" (19 tokens).

# GoogleTest's own statement on test order, shuffle/seed reproducibility, and per-test fixtures

## What was observed

The snapshot (2457 lines, sha256 05546ed6…, opened 2026-10-25 at commit cd8e73f067129f8489e35c7b51c7a68552b289d2) states three things that bear directly on the lane's F3 determinism frontier.

**Test order is undefined and the design must not depend on it.** "Remember that the test order is undefined, so your code can't depend on a test" (`googletest-advanced.md:896`); the sentence continues "preceding or following another. Also, the tests must either not modify the state" (`:897`), and the rule closes with "state to its original value before passing control to the next test." (`:899`).

**The framework ships a shuffle and publishes the seed.** "This helps to reveal bad dependencies between tests." (`:1977`) — the stated purpose of the `--gtest_shuffle` flag (`:1975`). "By default, GoogleTest uses a random seed calculated from the current time." (`:1979`). The console output includes "the random seed value, such that you can reproduce an order-related test failure" (`:1981`), and the seed is settable explicitly: "To specify the random seed explicitly, use the `--gtest_random_seed=SEED`" (`:1982`).

**A new test fixture object is created per test.** "GoogleTest creates a new test fixture object for each test in order to make" (`:872`) "tests independent and easier to debug." (`:873`). The same section notes the one-copy-per-test model can be prohibitively expensive for shared resources (`:874-875`) and then describes the static-member `SetUpTestSuite()`/`TearDownTestSuite()` sharing alternative (`:881-888`) — i.e., the per-test isolation is the default, and sharing is an explicit opt-in.

## What is inferred

- **The seed is the run's ordering identity; publishing it is the reproducibility mechanism.** Because the order is undefined (`:896`) and the default seed is derived from the current time (`:1979`), two runs cannot be compared by order alone; the seed value printed by the console (`:1981`) is exactly what allows a later reproduction, and the explicit `--gtest_random_seed=SEED` form (`:1982`) pins it. This matches the lane's own frontier: `repeated-control-precondition.md` records that `controls_match` documents observed stream stability while determinism is a property of the program across runs, including runs not taken; and `hermetic-env-differential.md` hashes raw streams with `normalization: none` (no path or time is replaced), so a run-identity value such as a time-derived seed that reaches stdout would read as `nondeterministic` there. GoogleTest's answer to that class is to *publish* the identity (print the seed) and let the caller pin it, not to strip it from the compared output; the lane's instrument does neither today, which is a limit of the lane, not a claim the snapshot makes.
- **Shuffle is a detection mechanism for the lane's hazard class, not a nuisance.** "This helps to reveal bad dependencies between tests." (`:1977`) names "bad dependencies between tests"; the lane reads that as the same hazard class as the author-side rule (an inference, not the snapshot's wording) "preceding or following another. Also, the tests must either not modify the state" (`:897`) / "state to its original value before passing control to the next test." (`:899`) — and treats a *randomised* order as the mechanism that exposes it.
- **The per-test fixture object is the mechanism-side complement to the author-side rule.** `:872-873` describes the fixture-per-test model as making tests independent and easier to debug; `:897-899` states the author-side obligation. Together they ground the lane's assumption that test isolation is a framework-supported default, not merely an author convention.
- **Normative status, finite scope.** As with `repeated-control-precondition.md`'s treatment of its sources, the snapshot states rules and mechanisms; it does not establish that any particular implementation obeys them, and this entry claims only what the snapshot's bytes support.

## Limits

- The snapshot is one document at one commit (cd8e73f067129f8489e35c7b51c7a68552b289d2). Fetched live on 2026-10-25, the same URL's bytes hash to the same sha256 (05546ed6…) and diff clean against the snapshot (diff exit 0); the `master` alias hashes identically, and `git ls-remote --heads https://github.com/google/googletest` on 2026-10-25 showed `refs/heads/main` at `cd8e73f…` (the branch list has no `master`; the raw `master` alias still resolves) — the row stays pinned to the commit, not to a branch name.

# Most observed pass-to-fail transitions involve a flaky test, by the publisher's own numbers

## What the snapshot states

S260 is the publisher's per-post Atom feed. The post body is the HTML string at `entry.content.$t`; the snapshot is one JSON line (0 newlines, 8,353 bytes, sha256 `434d8658…`), so citations below name the field, not a line number. The feed's `entry.link[rel=alternate].href` names `https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html` — the rendered page this lane already holds as S026 — so the feed is a second carrier of the same document, not a second document: the two rows state the same figure, and opening the feed adds no claim the page does not carry. The lane's extractor reads the post body from either carrier (the rendered page holds it twice, in a `text/template` copy and a `<noscript>` copy; `corpus/knowledge/repeated-control-precondition.md:3`). The reason to hold the feed as well is a pin: the rendered page's live bytes change between fetches (the round-45 re-fetch found S026's live bytes different from its snapshot, `corpus/lessons/round-45-verifier-spotcheck.md` C1 re-check), while the per-post record re-fetched byte-identical in round 46 (`.ufo/waves/round-46/w2/T46ExecLive.md`).

**Definition and corpus rate.** A flaky result is "a test that exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code" (15 words); across the corpus "we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a" (14 words) flaky result. The post ties the rate to the fix rate: "the insertion rate is about the same as the fix rate" (11 words).

**Reach.** "Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them" (13 words); equivalently "more than 1 in 7 of the tests written by our world-class engineers occasionally fail" (15 words) in a way not caused by changes to the code or tests.

**Post-submit transitions.** The CI system flags a passing test that transitions to failing so the submission can be investigated, and "about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test" (15 words). The lane's S026-ground entry `corpus/knowledge/repeated-control-precondition.md` already quotes this sentence from the rendered page; the feed states it in the same words.

**The default mitigation is a rerun in later CI cycles — the identification step, priced as a delay.** "build monitors typically wait for additional CI cycles to run this test again to determine whether or not the test has been broken" (23 words), "adding to the delay of identifying real problems and increasing the pool of changes that could contribute" (17 words). At project scale the arithmetic is the post's: "If 1.5% of test results are flaky, 15 tests will likely fail" (12 words) in "the average project contains 1000 or so individual tests" (9 words).

**A declared-flaky mechanism, with its latency stated.** The post's declared-flaky option is "causing it to report a failure only if it fails 3 times in a row" (15 words); "This reduces false positives, but encourages developers to ignore flakiness in their own tests" (14 words). The wait is explicit: "The breakage will not be discovered until 3 executions of the test complete, or 45 minutes" (16 words) for a 15-minute integration test, after which the post says it must still be settled "or if the test just flaked three times in a row" (11 words).

**Masking, stated as an observed habit rather than a hypothesis.** "It is quite common to ignore legitimate failures in flaky tests due to the high number of false-positives" (18 words), generalised as "It is human nature to ignore alarms when there is a history of false signals coming from a system" (19 words). The quarantine strategy is named together with what it hides: "A tool that monitors the flakiness of tests and if the flakiness is too high, it automatically quarantines the test" (20 words), which "could easily mask a real race condition or some other bug in the code being tested" (16 words).

**The publisher's own direction.** "we are seeing promising correlations with features that should enable us to identify a flaky result accurately" (17 words) without re-running the test — an aspiration in the post, not a measured result.

## What is inferred

- **Inference — the false-red prior.** If about 84% of observed pass→fail transitions in a large corpus involve a flaky test, one red observation in that corpus is weak evidence of a defect, and a verdict rule run on a corpus with that transition rate would carry a comparable false-red share unless it states an attempt budget or an independent witness. Whether this lane's own legs — single-run probes of deterministic fixtures, counted by `corpus/QUALITY.md` criterion 82 as killed when a completed run fails a declared check — have any such share is not measured here.
- **Inference — rerun as deferred identification.** The post's rerun is the identification step ("to determine whether or not the test has been broken"), deferred to later CI cycles; the cost the post names is the delay. Its declared-flaky option needs three consecutive failures before it reports one, and even then the post says the question remains whether the test is broken or "just flaked three times in a row": an attempt count bounds the wait, not the determination.
- **Inference — the discovery-latency term.** Attempts multiply test duration: the post's 15-minute test becomes 45 minutes at three attempts. A per-attempt rerun budget is therefore priced in executions × duration, and that term is bounded by the test's runtime, not by the flake rate.
- **Inference — suppression without a stated floor converts a known failure into an ignored one.** Because developers are reported to ignore legitimate failures among flaky ones, a cadence that suppresses red builds without a stated detection floor moves a real failure into the ignored class. The floor is the condition under which the cadence is being paid for at all, so it belongs in the claim, not in the report.
- **Inference — a prior on the lane's own variance.** The same figure is a prior on how much of the lane's measured run-to-run variance is worth chasing: in a large corpus a red that does not reproduce is the expected case, which is why the lane's F3 repeated-control entry treats one clean control as finite-sample agreement rather than as proof of determinism.

- One company's post-submit suite, at its scale, in 2016. The denominator is not this lane's gate fleet, and nothing here measures the lane's own false-red rate.

None of those figures is restated: the lane holds no row carrying those prices, and this snapshot states no such numbers. What is kept is only the ratio the snapshot itself states.
- F3 stays open. This entry supplies the false-red prior a flaky-aware verdict is judged against; it does not measure the lane's controls, and it does not raise the frontier's status.

# A receipt is evidence only for the content it was measured against (round 56)

An attestation is about a subject it identifies by digest: "Set of software
artifacts that the attestation applies to. Each element MUST have `digest` set",
and "Subject artifacts are matched purely by digest, regardless of content type"
(S281 §Fields, `subject`; the second sentence is the located quote, lines 54-55).
The lane's receipts are attestations of the same shape, one layer down: a control,
a positive control or a counter verdict is evidence about a *revision*, and a
receipt that names a different revision — or none — is evidence about something
else. Until round 56 the lane never checked that, and two accepted receipts were
exactly the defect the sentence names.

## The rule

A receipt is admitted as evidence only for the content it was measured against.
Concretely, every receipt a round certifies carries in its own bytes the revision
it was measured against (`rev=<sha>` or `"rev": "<sha>"`), and the lane's
certification path runs `tools/receipt-revision-gate.py` over it:

```
python3 tools/receipt-revision-gate.py --lane LANE --certified REV \
        [--paths SURFACE.txt] --receipt PATH:ROLE[:REQUIRE_REGEX] [--receipt …] [--json]
```

`REV` is the certified (measured) revision. `ROLE` is one of:

| role | what it admits | rule |
|---|---|---|
| `positive` | a control whose expected verdict is PASS | exactly one distinct `rev=`; it must equal `REV`, or — only with `--paths` — name a revision whose bytes are identical to `REV` on every listed path |
| `verdict` | a counter's verdict receipt | identical to `positive` (the code takes the two roles in one branch) |
| `control` | a control set with several `CTL` lines | every `rev=` token must resolve and be an ancestor of, or equal to, `REV`; `--paths` is not consulted |

One verdict line, and only that line is the verdict:
`GATE: receipts=N ok=N refused=N codes=<comma|none> verdict=PASS|REFUSED`.
Exit 0 iff `PASS`; exit 3 is a named refusal; exit 2 is
`GATE: error=unresolvable-certified … codes=RECEIPT_REV_UNRESOLVABLE`, a
could-not-evaluate — the gate did not run. The codes are a closed list of eleven
(`RECEIPT_MISSING`, `RECEIPT_EMPTY`, `RECEIPT_NOT_BLOB`, `RECEIPT_REV_ABSENT`,
`RECEIPT_REV_AMBIGUOUS`, `RECEIPT_REV_UNRESOLVABLE`, `RECEIPT_REV_MISMATCH`,
`RECEIPT_REV_CONTENT_DRIFT`, `RECEIPT_CONTROL_NOT_ANCESTOR`,
`RECEIPT_DIGEST_MISMATCH`, `RECEIPT_REQUIRED_LINE_MISSING`); the tool's own
selftest asserts the list is closed (case `codes-closed`).

The tool reads git objects and receipt bytes only. It writes nothing and allocates
no scratch outside `TMPDIR`; the lane's deciding runner extracts its bytes with
`git show REV:tools/receipt-revision-gate.py` and runs that copy, so the gate a
round is judged by is the gate the round froze.

## What it catches — three receipts the lane had already accepted
